records.title: E-140: the tick paths stop writing the frame's counters per entity, minimalTick?props=130000 logic −8.7 %
records.text:
The logic loop wrote the frame's counters on `this` for every ticked entity: `entitiesProcessedThisFrame++` in the bucket walk and in both single-entity paths, and `_lastTickMs` / `_lastDecimateMs` reset per entity although only detailed stats read them. Every path already returned what it counted, so the frame's count is now added once from `activeCount`, and the two timers are reset only with detailed stats on (9601cb65).

**Owner, minimalTickScene?props=130000** (0e50c580 adds the knob: 60 000 props put logic at 1.8 ms, under the floor; past 65 535 the scene runs without physics, which Box2D would refuse). 4 pairs from worktrees, the knob commit against the change: logic 4.654 → 4.271 ms (**−8.7 %**, worse 1/4, cv 19/6 %). The worse pair is one baseline side at 3.06 ms, below every other side of the sitting (A 4.59–4.79, B 3.95–4.56), so the base's spread is that side; the other three pairs are −14.0, −12.5 and −4.9 %. Spatial +0.0 %, pre-render −0.4 %, presented 60.0 both; ENTITIES_PROCESSED 130 000 on both sides (the count is unchanged). **Kept.** No A/A this session for this scene.

An earlier sitting at 60 000 props (logic 1.825 → 1.995 ms, below the floor) is void: the node suite ran during one of its sides.

records.title: E-146: onCollisionStay only for classes that define it, contact kernel +64 % / +34 %
records.text:
The stay walk in `_processBox2dCollisionCallbacks` called `onCollisionStay` for every type that listens to collisions, so a class that overrides only `onCollisionEnter` (waterAndBoxes' water balls, Predator's rain drops) had the base class's empty `onCollisionStay` called for each of its touching pairs, every frame. The change keeps a second per-type table, `collisionStayByType`, set only when the class defines `onCollisionStay` below `GameObject` (the same test that decides `onMessage` and `onAnimationEnd`), and the stay walk reads that one (9bf13f33).

**Kernel** (`contactsMicrobench --no-stays`, 0fcd7168: the contact flow through the real logic worker with classes that define no `onCollisionStay`): two runs a side, the parent (9601cb65) against the change: 7 800 pairs 8.45–8.69 → 13.89–14.27 ops/s (+64 %), 42 861 pairs 1.51–1.60 → 1.98–2.20 ops/s (+34 %). Classes that define it are timed as before (8.7 and 1.5 ops/s).

**Owner, waterAndBoxesScene** (4 pairs from worktrees, the parent against the change): logic 1.833 → 1.378 ms (−23.1 %, 4/4 lower, cv 5/6 %), below the 3 ms floor, so not judged; the scene has no load knob. Spatial −0.8 %, physics +1.1 %, renderer +1.3 %, pre-render −4.2 %, presented 60.0 both. The scene is not worse, so the kernel claim stands: **kept.** No A/A this session for this scene.

records.title: E-109: updateLighting writes its texels itself, Predator Pixi 443.2 → 342 KB/s
records.text:
The heap pass of 2026-10-23 listed Pixi's `updateLighting` at 0.2–0.3 MB/s in Predator. It decoded each light's colour into `_rgbResult`'s fields (three heap numbers per light per frame in Chrome) and wrote the light's texel through `packLightDataTexel`, a call with seven doubles.

**First version** (colours into locals, here and at the three other per-light colour reads: the visibility-polygon lights, the self-lit batch, its sprite masks): `heapSampleWorkers`, Predator, Pixi worker, 10 s warm-up, 8 s sample: `updateLighting` 93.7 → 79.5 KB/s. Still there: the call was left out, so its double arguments were boxed instead.

**Kept version** (c8c3fc6a: `updateLighting` writes the texel itself; `packLightDataTexel` stays as the layout the tests read): `updateLighting` 93.7 KB/s → not listed; Pixi in all 443.2 → 342 KB/s. The rest is Pixi's own code (`bind` 90 KB/s, `push`, `startRenderPass`, `emit`). Garbage only, no time claim: the Predator gate over this and E-140 and E-146 passed (no worker worse; every worker lower, physics most, which is drift).

Left of the 2026-10-23 leads: game-code instance fields (documented in `bible_of_weed_js.md`, fed06cbc), Pixi's vendored `bind`, `_emscripten_get_now` (E-144) and `syncParticleFeed`.

records.title: Predator gate over E-140, E-146 and E-109
records.text: Predator, 4 pairs from worktrees, ce52192d against c8c3fc6a (E-140, E-146's collision dispatch and E-109's `updateLighting` together), detailed stats off: logic 3.821 → 3.663 ms (−3.3 %, worse 0/4, cv 2/2 %, +0.8 % against the other workers), spatial −2.0 %, physics −8.4 % (cv 5/7 %), renderer −2.9 %, pre-render −2.1 %, presented 60.0 both; BODY_COUNT and GPU_CASTERS within 0.3 %. Every worker moved down, physics most, and none of the three changes reaches physics: drift. Against it logic is level, so the gate says no worker got worse, not that Predator gained. **Passed.**

records.title: E-146: FSM.tick reads onUpdate from a per-class array and the ms per tick once, kernel +6.4 % / +11.3 %
records.text:
The FSM half of E-146. `FSM.tick` read the current state's `onUpdate` from the state class (Predator: 17 state classes over three FSMs, so that load saw 17 maps) and the time step from `owner.constructor.tickInterval` on every tick.

**Kernel** (`fsmTickMicrobench`, b26281f6: three FSM classes with Predator's state counts, 3, 9 and 5; two owner classes with its tickIntervals, 4 and 6, each ticking an animation FSM and a behaviour FSM; transitions at a few per hundred ticks; one variant per process, alternating, the checksum after 600 ticks equal for every variant):

| variant | 3000 owners (6 rounds) | 1000 owners (5 rounds) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| shipped | 6 477.5 ops/s | 19 420.1 |
| `onUpdate` from a per-class array | −8.3 % (3000, 5 rounds) | −1.8 % |
| the ms per tick cached on the FSM instance | +3.1 % | −0.1 % |
| both | **+6.4 %** | **+11.3 %** |

Each half alone ties or loses; together they win, at both counts. **Kept** (bc478827): each FSM class keeps its states' `onUpdate` by state number (built where the states are linked) and calls it with the state class as `this`; each FSM instance keeps its owner's ms per tick (`_msPerTick`, NaN until the first tick, declared in a constructor). With a dt of 1 the times are bit-identical; with another dt the product is formed in another order (one rounding apart). Scene: the Predator gate below; the FSM is 7 % of Predator's logic, so a 6–11 % kernel gain is under 1 % there, below what a sitting sees.

records.title: E-157: WebGL GPU particles from a texture, GPU Galaxy 1M 18 → 60 fps (the attributes were the cost)
records.text:
The suspect was the upload (a per-frame `bufferSubData` into a ring the GPU still draws from). It was not.

**Kernel** (`webglParticleUploadKernel`, 2f27006d, run headed with `chromeKernel --headed`, ba236be8; GTX 1650, Chrome on ANGLE D3D11; N instanced quads from one buffer of 112-byte records, the engine's layout). 1 048 576 records, 3 rounds, synchronous frame time (1-pixel `readPixels`) and frames presented:
- no upload at all: 50.9 ms, 18.5 fps; the frame's 3 500 records by `bufferSubData` 51.4 ms; through a staging buffer and `copyBufferSubData` 51.4 ms; drawn as two ranges with the attributes re-pointed 55.5 ms; the whole 117 MB every frame 85.6 ms. **The upload is not the cost; the draw is.**
- What the draw costs: the attribute count. Seven vec4 attributes 51.1 ms, six 46.0, five 41.1, three 25.3, one 11.6 (unread attributes made shader constants). A triangle strip instead of 6 indices (52.1), quads a quarter the size (52.1) and no blending (51.0) change nothing. About 7 ms per instanced attribute per million records: ANGLE's D3D11 fetches instance attributes slowly.
- **The records in an RGBA32F texture**, seven texels each, read with `texelFetch` by `gl_InstanceID`: **6.1 ms**, 60 fps; with the frame's rows sent by `texSubImage2D` 7.7 ms. 8.4 times the attributes.

**The change** (e6ee4ed3): on WebGL each ring's records are an RGBA32UI texture (seven texels a record, rows of 512, the ring's own copy as the texels; integer, so the bit fields go through a bitcast), filled by row with raw GL as the lookup textures are; the vertex shader is gpuParticle.vert.glsl with the seven attributes turned into globals it fetches from record `uFirstInstance + gl_InstanceID`, the first record a uniform of each mesh (each mesh has its own shader sharing the ring's resources and clock). WebGPU keeps its instance buffer.

**GPU Galaxy** `?backend=webgl&particles=1048576`, headed, 6 s warm-up, 8 s measured, two runs a side, alternating, the parent (worktree) against the change: frames drawn **144 and 141 → 480 and 480** (18 → 60 fps, the display's); the renderer's CPU step 0.80 → 0.50 ms. With the change 2 097 152 and 4 194 304 particles also draw at 60 fps on WebGL. Checked by screenshots: GPU Galaxy on WebGL against WebGPU, and gpuParticlesStressScene on WebGL with `sort=1` (groups drawn among y-sorted trees, each from its own first record) against WebGPU, and with `look=1`. Node tests: the shader transform on the real source, rows sent per frame, both pieces across the ring end, each mesh's first record (tests/node/gpuParticleBatch.test.js).

**Kept.**

records.title: E-144: the clock readers are sched_yield in waits; yielding every 64th spin NEUTRAL on ballsHeavy
records.text:
Who reads the clock, found without a names build: under Emscripten `b2Yield` is `sched_yield()`, and Emscripten's `sched_yield` is `_emscripten_yield(emscripten_get_now())` (emsdk `system/lib/libc/musl/src/sched/sched_yield.c`): a clock import call and a mailbox check. `b2Pause` is empty in WASM. Two loops yield: the solver workers' stage wait (`b2SolverTask`, every 6th spin) and the physics thread's task wait (`b2SchedulerFinishTask`, every idle pass). The scheduler's own spin already reads the clock every 64th spin (3b2d4c8).

**The variant** (Box2D repo, not committed): both loops yield every 64th spin under Emscripten, native builds unchanged. The SIMD and no-SIMD builds both passed (`build_for_weed.bat`). A clean build of Box2D's HEAD first reproduced WeedJS's shipped `box2dWasm.wasm` byte for byte (an incremental build had not: a stale build directory, 49 bytes off), so the pair compares only this change.

**ballsHeavyStressScene** (owner physics, 4 pairs from worktrees): physics 8.606 → 8.692 ms (+1.4 %, worse 3/4, cv 2/2 %), presented 60.0 both; the other workers under the floor. **NEUTRAL: not kept.** WeedJS's module and Box2D's sources are back at their HEADs.

As step 0 said: the threads that read the clock are waiting for work, off the critical path; reading it less does not shorten physics' step. What is left of E-144 is the names build only if a profile shows the clock on the physics thread's own critical path.

records.title: E-147 step 1: rows rebuilt, republished and skipped per frame in five spatial scenes
records.text:
Step 1 of E-147: how many neighbour rows each spatial scene rebuilds and republishes per frame. `NEIGHBORS_REBUILT` and `NEIGHBORS_PUBLISHED` (5803ca42) are written with the frame's other counters, detailed stats off. One run per scene, headed, from source, 6 s warm-up and 5 s measured, averages per spatial worker per frame. Rebuilt rows go through the gather and the publish; rows kept within the skin skip the gather but are published again; stagger-skipped rows (`neighborTickInterval`) skip both.

| Scene | spatial step | rows | rebuilt | kept by skin, republished | stagger-skipped |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Boids (2 workers) | 6.2 ms | 20 000 | 6.7 % | 0 % | 93.3 % |
| orientedBoxScene | 3.7 ms | 1 044 | 99.1 % | 0.9 % | 0 % |
| Predator | 4.8 ms | 17 583 | 3.7 % | 5.9 % | 89.5 % |
| movedBodiesMixedScene | 4.1 ms | 22 000 | 1.0 % | 99.0 % | 0 % |
| stationarySpatialWideScene (2 workers) | 11.3 ms | 35 000 | 3.9 % | 96.1 % | 0 % |

What it says:
- **Boids and Predator** already skip nine rows in ten with the stagger. Boids' gather (44 % of its spatial) is the 6.7 % it rebuilds: few rows, each expensive.
- **orientedBoxScene** rebuilds every row every frame although the default skin (0.04) is on: `_canReuseNeighbors` requires the entity's half extent unchanged, and a rotating box's bounding box changes every frame. Neither range test uses the entity's own extent (the gather adds the candidate's to the search range, the publish the candidate's to the visual range), so the check stands in for "the shapes changed". Relaxing it would have to budget the candidates' extent growth inside the skin (a 200 px box grows by up to 100 px as it turns, against a 12 px skin), or neighbours go missing for up to 15 frames: a correctness trade, a lead, not done.
- **movedBodiesMixed and stationarySpatialWide** republish 96–99 % of their rows from candidate lists kept within the skin: that republish is their publish share (46 % and 61 %). The rows of entities that did not move, among candidates that did not move, come out the same each time: E-136's regime, wider than "static entities with large visual ranges" (stationarySpatialWide's entities are not `isStatic`; movedBodiesMixed has the grid's mover list on 96 % of frames). In the stationary scene the rebuilt 3.9 % is the list-age cap (`maxReuseFrames`) alone.

So the "less work" left to E-147 is in the publish of kept rows (E-136, generalised: skip a kept row when neither its entity nor a candidate moved since its last publish), not in the gather. Predator publishes 5.9 % of its rows that way, so the gain is in the stress scenes, not in Predator.

records.title: Predator gate over the FSM, the WebGL record texture and the spatial row counters
records.text: Predator, 4 pairs from worktrees, 7445a6a6 against e6ee4ed3 (E-146's FSM tick, the spatial row counters of E-147 and E-157's WebGL record texture together), detailed stats off: logic 3.688 → 3.645 ms (−1.2 %, worse 1/4, cv 3/2 %), spatial −2.1 %, physics −5.1 % (cv 2/12 %), renderer −5.6 % (cv 9/4 %), pre-render −3.5 %, presented 60.0 both; BODY_COUNT and GPU_CASTERS within 0.4 %. NEUTRAL: no worker worse, every one lower, physics among them, which none of these changes reaches (drift). Predator draws no GPU particles, so its renderer says nothing about E-157. **Passed.**

records.title: E-158 screened: a single triangle loses to the quad and the vertex math is 0.5 ms at 4 million
records.text:
Screened in the WebGL kernel (`webglParticleUploadKernel`, `tri` and `heavy`, 6749b471; headed, GTX 1650, ANGLE D3D11), 4 194 304 records read from the record texture as the engine now does (E-157), 2 rounds, the synchronous frame time per round:

| draw | light vertex | `heavy` vertex (six eases, a rotation, a drag curve) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| a quad: 4 vertices, 2 triangles (the engine) | 12.4 / 7.3 ms | 12.9 / 7.8 ms |
| one triangle around the quad, 3 vertices, outside discarded | 13.0 / 8.0 ms | 13.3 / 8.4 ms |

All at 60 fps. The rounds differ by 5 ms (the GPU's clocks), but inside each round the triangle is slower than the quad, and the engine's kind of vertex work adds about 0.5 ms at 4 million. So the per-vertex evaluation is not what a GPU particle costs: one evaluation per particle (a WebGPU compute pass) would save a fraction of 0.5 ms, and the single triangle loses on its larger raster. What grows with the count is the record fetch and the raster of tiny quads. **Screened.** Since E-157 both backends draw 4 million at 60 fps on this GPU.

records.title: E-109 closed: syncParticleFeed was fixed by E-149, the clock is E-144's, Pixi's bind is Pixi's
records.text: The last leads of the 2026-10-23 heap pass. `syncParticleFeed` (0.1–0.2 MB/s then) walked the changed bits through two closures a call; E-149 wrote the walks out (a2398952, PR #5), so it is gone. `_emscripten_get_now` in the Box2D threads is E-144's: its readers are `sched_yield` in the solver's waits, off the critical path, and yielding less was NEUTRAL in time (R-0675). Pixi's vendored `bind` (90 KB/s in Predator after c8c3fc6a) is Pixi's own per-draw code once E-148 took its `for…in` out. With `updateLighting` done (R-0671) and the instance-field rule written (fed06cbc), nothing of the pass is open.

records.title: E-140: types without a RigidBody skip the acceleration resets, minimalTick logic −18.0 %
records.text:
Every tick path reset the entity's three accelerations (`RigidBody.ax`, `ay`, `angularAccel`: physics applies them each step until the next tick), whether or not its type has a RigidBody. RigidBody's arrays exist for every entity (a core component), so the stores were in bounds, and wasted for every type without a body.

**The upper bound first** (a throwaway commit that dropped the three stores in the every-frame path, never merged): minimalTickScene?props=130000 (its props have no RigidBody), 4 pairs: logic 4.138 → 3.202 ms (−22.4 %, worse 0/4). Far more than three stores should cost; worth the copies.

**The change**: a type without a RigidBody takes its own copies, chosen once per type so no branch enters the loops (the hot-loop rule): `_tickNonDecimatedTypeNoBody` (update()'s two loops, forced and block range) with `_tickNonDecimatedOneNoBody`, and `_tickBucketNoBody` for the tickInterval buckets. Types with a body run exactly the code they ran. tests/node/tickNoBody.test.js: both kinds tick every entity, in both paths; the accelerations reset only with a body (the old code fails it).

**minimalTickScene?props=130000** (4 pairs from worktrees, the parent against the change): logic **4.088 → 3.382 ms (−18.0 %, worse 0/4, cv 6/4 %)**; spatial −2.4 %. **minimalTickIntervalBucketScene** (160 000 props, tickInterval 4, the bucket path): logic 2.683 → 2.130 ms (−20.6 %), below the 3 ms floor, not judged; spatial −2.2 %. **Kept.** Predator gate (4 pairs, 9ed173d0 against the change): NEUTRAL, logic 3.705 → 3.760 ms (+0.8 %, worse 2/4); physics +6.1 % but worse in 2 of 4 pairs, and it cannot be reached (the stores left out belong to entities without a Box2D body): noise, within Predator's 8–13 % per worker. Passed.

records.title: DX-SW phase 3: a deploy's first visit +125 ms once, return visits and runtime as real headers; narrow kept, SW-9 not needed
records.text:
Phase 3 of the isolation service worker plan, measured 2026-10-28 (Chrome 156, GTX 1650, headed).

**Load time** (`isolationLoadTime.mjs`, 1ade2dea and e8f4ba74): from the navigation to the renderer's first published frame (frameTotals, read by the page every animation frame, on the same wall clock), 10 runs a row in rotating order, a fresh context a run, one unrecorded warm-up visit first. Medians (p25–p75), ms:

| Page | Visit | Real headers | weed-sw.js (narrow) | wide (every response) | Static Routing (second sitting) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| bundle, dist/index.html with 300 balls | first | 572 (552–580) | 698 (681–707), reload at 179 | 713 (704–721) | 690 (677–699) |
| bundle | return | 429 (413–441) | 443 (432–447) | 446 (433–458) | 442 (429–465) |
| source, isolationSmoke.html | first | 1 151 | 1 664 | 1 877 | 1 708 |
| source | return | 1 063 | 1 431 | 1 680 | 1 432 |

In the second sitting real headers read 552 / 442 / 1 181 / 1 118 and the narrow worker 680 / 431 / 1 673 / 1 446.

- A deploy (the bundle): the first visit costs about 125 ms once; a return visit is within the noise of real headers. The plan's inline gate for the double parse is not worth it.
- Narrow against wide: a tie with the bundle; from source the wide worker is 17 % slower on a return visit. Decision 2 (page loads and worker scripts only) stands.
- SW-9: not needed. Besides the wide worker, Chrome's Static Routing API (tests/bench/isolation/weedSwRouted.js: page loads and worker scripts to the fetch handler, the rest to the network; Chrome accepted the rules, read from the running worker) ties the narrow worker.
- From source through the worker (`npm run dev:sw`) a return visit is 330–370 ms slower than real headers, and not because of the module requests' fetch events (the routed worker skips them and ties). Unexplained; the dev servers that send real headers do not meet it.

**Runtime** (`weedIsolation=sw` in runIntegratedWorkerBenchmark, f5eb5417): Predator, 4 pairs, one build, real headers against the worker on a return visit: logic +0.7 % (worse 2/4), spatial 0.0 %, renderer −3.1 %, pre-render −3.2 %, physics −5.9 % (cv 8/12 %), presented 60 both. No difference: the worker only touches loading.

records.title: DX-SW: a worker's module imports were rewritten too; leaving them alone brings a boot from source to real headers (1 415 → 1 114 ms, headers 1 071)
records.text:
Why a boot from source through weed-sw.js was 330–370 ms slower than real headers, found by narrowing:
- The page's timeline: the navigation and the worker scripts cost the same; the slow requests were the engine workers' module imports (Chrome lists them in the page's Resource Timing): 728 of them, 55 ms each (median) with real headers and 204 through the worker, every one with a workerStart.
- The main thread's own graph (175 modules, a page that only imports /src/index.js): 140–153 ms with real headers, without isolation, and controlled by the shipped worker, the routed one, one with an empty fetch handler and one with none. Being controlled costs nothing there.
- A probe worker recording each request: a module worker's imports have destination 'worker' (the HTML spec gives the module graph the worker's destination) and mode 'cors', no resulting client; a worker's own script has mode 'same-origin' and a resulting client (6 engine workers, 3 Box2D threads). So the filter for page loads and worker scripts rewrote all 728 imports, and the Static Routing rules (destination worker → fetch handler) did too.

**The fix** (417b5f0a): weed-sw.js rewrites page loads and worker scripts whose mode is not 'cors'. dist/weed-sw.js is the same bytes. tests/node/isolationServiceWorker.test.js: imports with destination worker or sharedworker and mode cors go to the network untouched; isolationWorkerSmoke 11/11.

**isolationLoadTime**, 10 runs (dbd1e427: weedSwImports.js, the same condition, against the shipped worker in one sitting), medians: from source, return visit real headers 1 071 ms, before 1 415, after 1 114; first visit 1 159, 1 684, 1 363. Bundle: return 431 / 433 / 446, first 550 / 705 / 688 (its worker scripts are blobs). With Static Routing on top (weedSwImportsRouted.js) a 2-run screen tied (1 107 against 1 087), so it is not shipped.

records.title: H-ROW / H-OWN screened: the rebuild's skipped entities are not its cost
records.text: One index per row or one owned list lowers `spatialMax` ≥3% when the rebuild or the home-row skip dominate. — 30k rebuild 1.518 / step 10.409 (14%). 300k rebuild 13.235 / step 145.427 (9%); neighbor 132.182. Home-row skip 7.5% and 7.1%. … 2026-10-28 (spatialRebuildWasmMicrobench, Predator mix, 16 500 entities, 4 rounds): a worker's rebuild costs as much with two or three workers as one worker's doing every row (357, 426, 363 µs a frame each), yet leaving other workers' circles before reading their columns wins +3.2 % with two workers and loses 21.2 % with one; the cell range inline +6.4 % and −7.6 %; W6's C port +2.0 % and −2.2 %. The rebuild is not in the entities a worker skips.

records.title: W7 screened: the spatial glue is about 8 % of the frame, its counters and the rebuild in C tie
records.text:
W7 (one WebAssembly call per frame for the spatial rebuild, gather and publish) was blocked on the components living in one memory, which the WASM migration finished. Screened before porting, on what it could save:

- **The share of the glue.** A CPU profile of spatialGatherWasmMicrobench (Predator's settings, 3 workers): of the spatial frame, gather_batch about 43 %, rebuildOwnedRows 29 %, the JS decision loop in _findNeighbors about 8 %, publish_batch 7 %. (The profile charges about 12 % to JS-to-WASM transitions, which three calls a worker a frame cannot cost; it attributes WASM time to the wrappers.) So the JS a port would remove is about 8 % of the frame, and a C version of the same decisions still costs part of that.
- **The rebuild in C** (W6) ties: +2.0 % and −2.2 % with one and two workers in spatialRebuildWasmMicrobench (2026-10-28), as in its first screen.
- **The loop's own writes.** It wrote three counters per entity on `this` and the publish object, as logic's tick paths did before E-140 (−8.7 % there). In locals instead (written once a frame): the kernel ties, −0.2 % on Predator's settings and −0.9 % on a frame that rebuilds every list, checksums equal (6 alternating rounds a tree, the parent against the change from worktrees). Not committed.

**Screened**: a port's ceiling is a few per cent of spatial, under what a sitting resolves, for a large change. The spatial frame is the gather and the rebuild; see E-147.

records.title: E-147: the gather in float32x4 wins Chrome's replay (+9–12 %, exact) but Boids is 3.0 % worse: not shipped
records.text:
The Chrome entry for the gather's float32 variants (E-147's step 2), and the shipped gather that came of it.

**How Chrome was asked.** The gather's Node kernel builds real spatial workers in Node, which a page cannot. So `spatialGatherSnapshot.mjs` (2466cb37) runs that kernel (16 500 entities, 3 workers) and captures one frame: every worker's `gather_batch` call and the WebAssembly memory after it (grid, poses, ranges, the batch lists). `spatialGatherReplayKernel.mjs` replays it in Chrome (chromeKernel, Chrome 156) on the same bytes with each variant, a fresh frame stamp per replay, rounds alternating, and compares every candidate row with the shipped gather's. Two captures: every list rebuilt (13 743 rows a frame, the gather's own cost) and Predator's skin and stagger (933 rows).

**The variants in Chrome**, ms per replayed frame (median of 9 rounds), against the shipped double gather:

| capture | double (shipped) | f32 | f32x4 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| every list rebuilt | 18.174 | 17.594 (+3.3 %) | 16.450 (**+10.5 %**) |
| Predator's | 1.365 | 1.331 (+2.6 %) | 1.263 (**+8.1 %**) |

No candidate row differed in either capture. Node had f32x4 at −1.2 % (R-0571): Chrome decides, and it differs.

**Exact, not just tolerated.** f32x4 ported into `wasm/spatialGather.c` alone kept the speed but not the bits: a frame with a skin of 0 (the gather's edge is the publish's) and rows at their 64-candidate cap published a different set in the 32-bit parity test, and the rebuild kernel's checksum changed. A margin on the squared range (a superset of the candidates) fixed neither, since an extra edge candidate moves a truncated row's cut. The exact form decides in float32 only outside a band of 2^-19 (relative, on the squared range) around the edge; a candidate inside it, which the tolerance analysis bounds at about 5e-7 relative, takes the double test JS does. So the gather keeps exactly what the double gather keeps: the node suite unchanged and green (2 084), and spatialGatherWasmMicrobench's checksums unchanged (predator 2053291771, rebuild 1527620844).

**The exact form in Chrome** (the replay with the previous engine.wasm as `before`): every list rebuilt 17.747 → 16.261 ms (**+9.1 %**), Predator's 1.307 → 1.172 ms (**+11.5 %**); rows identical. The same speed as the plain f32x4 (+8.3 %, +11.8 % in that sitting): the band costs nothing measurable.

A second form kept the double test also past a cell's last block of four (a cell of three or fewer is then all double): +9.0 % and +12.2 % against the old gather in Chrome, rows identical.

**The scenes** (4 pairs each from worktrees, owner spatial, the commit before the gather against it):
- orientedBoxScene (gather 76 % of its spatial): 3.647 → 3.552 ms (−2.3 %, worse 0/4), and with the second form 3.529 → 3.431 ms (−2.3 %, worse 0/4).
- Boids (gather 44 %, 20 px cells of at most 20 boids): +1.4 % (pairs −3.3 / +0.7 / +2.1 / +5.3), and with the second form 6.578 → 6.824 ms (**+3.0 %, worse 4/4**, cv 1/2 %).
- Predator (gather 37 %): 4.914 → 4.826 ms (−1.8 %, worse 1/4); physics +4.7 % (cv 7/6 %), which the gather cannot reach.

**Not shipped.** A kernel claim needs the kernel win and no scene 3 % worse, and Boids is 3.0 % worse in every pair: where cells hold few ids, a block of four loads and shuffles rows the scalar loop would have left at the first test. The exact form stays as a test module (`wasm/test/spatialGatherExact.c`, 2e7d42b2) and a replay variant (`exact`, +12.6 % on Predator's capture). A lead, not measured: the blocks only in cells with more ids (eight or more, say), where Predator's and orientedBox's cells are.

records.title: DX-SW phase 2: Firefox 3/3, audio, npm run dev 4/4; an isolated portal cannot embed a headerless host
records.text:
Phase 2's remaining rows, 2026-10-28.

- **Firefox** (isolationWorkerSmoke.mjs --browser firefox, 26c24b2e): the installed Firefox 159 driven over HTTP (stockFirefox.mjs; Playwright's Firefox is not Firefox's speed and is not installed). First visit: 2 loads, isolated, the scene running and drawing, weed-sw.js registered; return visit: 1 load; real headers: 1 load, nothing registered. 3/3. Two driver lessons: a call the page takes just before the first visit's reload is never answered (short asks, repeated), and a navigation the test asks for must wait for the answer to leave (300 ms).
- **Audio** (8a67ebe8): through the worker the engine's mixer node starts with its shared buffer, and a worklet loaded by URL as the mixer is (tests/bench/isolation/sabProbeProcessor.js) receives a SharedArrayBuffer posted to it (the value read back).
- **The allowed frame** (8a67ebe8): an isolated portal (real headers) embedding the game from a host without them, `allow="cross-origin-isolated"`: refused, `net::ERR_BLOCKED_BY_RESPONSE`. The parent's COEP needs CORP and COEP on the frame's response, which comes before weed-sw.js can be installed there, and a worker from a direct visit does not reach a third-party frame. A known limit, now asserted by the case and written in DEPLOY.md's "Game portals": a game in an isolated portal needs its host to send the headers (itch.io's SharedArrayBuffer option does).
- **npm run dev** (isolationDevSmoke.mjs, 8304e508): a script of the running scene written again is hot swapped, nothing navigates, no worker is registered; an asset written again reloads the page once with the scene's state kept. The same with a weed-sw.js left on the port by npm run dev:sw. 4/4.

The Chromium smoke is 13/13 with the new cases. Phase 4 (Safari, Chrome on Android, real deploys) is by hand.

records.text:

| worker | main → branch | paired | worse | vs the others |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| logic (owner) | 3.834 → 3.942 ms | +4.7 % | 3/4 | **−1.7 %** (lower 3/4) |
| spatial | 4.748 → 4.920 ms | +2.5 % | 4/4 | −0.5 % |

records.title: E-136 kept: kept rows left out of the publish while no pose changed
records.text:
E-136 in the wide form E-147's step 1 pointed at: a kept row is left out of the publish while no pose changed since its last publish (64899791).

**What changed.** The publish reads only the poses, the entity's range and its candidate list. A list kept within the skin is the same list, and its range is the one it was built with (`_canReuseNeighbors`), so the row comes out of the publish as it went in unless a pose moved. Each spatial worker compares the poses it writes with the ones already there, until one differs (the full rebuild, its latched copy and the movers rewrite), and after such a frame adds 2 to a generation in the publish memory's new `sync` region (Atomics, after the pose writes). Each row remembers the generation read before its last publish; a kept row whose generation is unchanged is skipped. A row cleared for a range of 0 is marked so it is published again. A layout without the region (hand-made metadata) keeps the old behaviour.

**Exact.** `tests/node/spatialKeptRowSkip.test.js` runs three workers on a still world with the engine's reuse defaults and a script (a move in worker 0's rows, a move only worker 2 writes, an extent change, a range to 0 and back, a move and back a frame apart, a step every third frame), and holds the rows to the run without the skip frame by frame. It catches two mutants: a generation per worker (another worker's pose unseen) and a cleared row not marked. Node suite 2 086 green, demos 100.

**Kernel** (spatialWorkerMicrobench, 3 workers, 16 500 entities, Node, 5 alternating rounds against 2ac7b1f9): still with skin 0.04 (`--still`, 2ac7b1f9's own commit) 149.0 → 52.0 ms per 20 frames (−65 %), checksum unchanged; Predator's drift 57.7 → 58.3 ms (+1 %), the compare in the full rebuild. Writing the worker's flag once after the loop instead of in it halved that cost (variants timed in the same sitting).

**Scenes**, 4 pairs each from worktrees, 2ac7b1f9 against 64899791's tree, owner spatial, detailed stats off:

| scene | spatial | worse | verdict |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| stationarySpatialWideScene | 11.539 → 5.163 ms (**−55.2 %**) | 0/4, cv 1/1 % | KEPT |
| movedBodiesMixedScene | 4.152 → 4.028 ms (−2.3 %) | 0/4, cv 1/1 % | NEUTRAL |
| Predator | 4.793 → 4.846 ms (+2.4 %) | 3/4, cv 2/3 % | see below |

movedBodiesMixed gains on the frames where physics published no move. In Predator every worker the change cannot reach read higher in that sitting (renderer +4.2 %, logic +2.1 %, pre-render +2.1 %): read against them, spatial is +0.3 %. The session's A/A (Predator, 747c388a on both sides, 4 pairs) reads spatial +0.1 %, renderer +0.3 %, pre-render +0.4 %, logic +2.0 % (cv 5 %) and physics −3.4 % (cv 8/12 %): the detection limit is about 2 % on spatial, renderer and pre-render, 3.5 % on logic and physics.

**Kept.** The regime is frames where no pose moved anywhere: a scene where something moves every frame gets nothing. A per-neighbourhood form (skip a row whose own candidates did not move) needs a check per candidate, about what the publish costs, so it is not pursued.

records.title: N-6 answered: tweens that follow their entity's worker, three forms, none shipped
records.text:
N-6: with two or more logic workers, a tween is advanced by the worker whose block of slots holds it, and its entity is ticked by the worker whose share of the type's list holds it, so the two can write the same prop from two threads. The fix the item names (tweens advanced by the worker that ticks the entity) was built in three forms and measured. None shipped.

**The owner scene.** `tweenStressScene ?workers=2&tick=1` (7be61a49): one alpha tween per entity, entities with an empty tick, two logic workers. It is the worst case: every tween is on a ticking entity. Sittings: 4 pairs from worktrees against 7be61a49, owner logic, detailed stats off. Logic is under the 3 ms floor at 65 535 entities, so 150 000 (32-bit ids) was sat too.

| form | where | before → after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| index by entity (rebuilt when the pool changes), each type's share advanced before its loop, entity then slots | scene, 65 535 | 1.411 → 2.104 ms (+49 %) |
| the same | scene, 150 000 | 2.783 → 4.976 ms (+79 %) |
| every slot walked in order, kept when its entity id is in this worker's range of the type's list | Chrome kernel, 150 000, one worker's share | 1.48 → 2.30 ms (+55 %) |
| the index, with each share's slots cached in list order (rebuilt when the index or the list moves) | Chrome kernel, 150 000 | 1.485 → 1.638 ms (+10 %) |
| the same | scene, 150 000 | 2.755 → 4.609 ms (+67 %) |

The first version (a call per entity) read 1.41 → 2.74 ms at 65 535. The kernel (`tweenShareKernel.mjs`, branch `n6-tween-owner`) runs on the page's thread; in the scene the same code costs several times more (traces: the cached share's loop 437 ms and `_apply` 370 ms per 4 s on a logic thread, against Tween.tick's 181 ms and 211 ms before), which the kernel does not reproduce. Every form gives the same alphas as the blocks (checksums), and the worker test (two instances on a pool laid out against their shares: every tween once a frame, by its entity's worker) passed for the index forms.

**Answered, not done.** The race only matters when a tween and the entity's own tick write the same prop; reading a tweened prop is fine, and one logic worker has no race. Against +49 % to +79 % of logic where tweens are many, the contract stays: it is now in `Tween.to`'s declaration (`types/weed.d.ts`) and in the guide's tween section, besides MEMORY_STRUCTURE's tween row. The attempt is kept on the local branch `n6-tween-owner` (the cached form, its test and its kernel).

records.title: N-74 answered: the world's arrays 4 MB further on do not move physics
records.text:
N-74: does the place of the engine block in Box2D's heap move physics? The block (the render-queue memory and its regions, Phase 4) is malloc'ed before the world, so a bigger region there moves every body and contact array the world allocates after it. W27's pair saw physics +3.6 % with its Adobe tables on (R-0589), and all WASM against all JS read +7 % on the same demo (R-0640), where the other workers also ran faster (L5).

**The pair that separates it.** One build (f3afbf83) on both sides, adobeAnimateScene at the minimum zoom, the only difference the Adobe tables' region: 4 MB on side A (the default), 8 MB on side B (`?adobeTablesMB=`, a demo knob), so side B's world arrays sit 4 MB further on. 4 pairs, `runPredatorAbab --vs f3afbf83 --query-a adobeTablesMB=4 --query-b adobeTablesMB=8 --owner physics --camera-zoom min`, detailed stats off.

| worker | A → B | paired | worse |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| physics (owner) | 6.009 → 5.988 ms | +1.2 % | 2/4, cv 3/3 % |
| pre-render | 10.768 → 10.826 ms | +0.5 % | 3/4 |
| renderer | 6.647 → 6.641 ms | −0.1 % | 2/4 |

BODY_COUNT 20 000 both. NEUTRAL: physics is within the session's noise (the A/A put physics at ±3.4 %).

**Answered.** Where the block puts the world does not move physics, so there is no knob to add; the +7 % against the JS engine is L5 (the other workers busier on the same cores). Nothing pending.

records.title: E-147's lead: float32x4 blocks only in cells of 8 or 16 ids, Boids still worse
records.text:
E-147's lead: the exact float32x4 gather (spatialGatherExact's form) shipped into `wasm/spatialGather.c` with its blocks of four only in cells that hold BLOCK_MIN_IDS ids or more, so Boids' few-id cells keep the double test throughout.

**Exact.** With the threshold at 8 and at 16 the node suite stays green and spatialGatherWasmMicrobench's checksums are unchanged (predator 2053291771, rebuild 1527620844): the rows are the double gather's.

**Boids first** (the scene the earlier form lost, +3.0 % from four ids), 4 pairs from worktrees against e3825d58, owner spatial, detailed stats off:

| BLOCK_MIN_IDS | spatial | worse | cv |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 8 | 6.696 → 6.754 ms (+1.4 %) | 4/4 | 1/1 % |
| 16 | 6.640 → 6.784 ms (+1.8 %) | 3/4 | 2/2 % |

Boids' cells hold at most 20 ids (maxEntitiesPerCell 20), so at 16 almost none take a block, and Boids is no better: what costs there is not the blocks alone. The likely remainder is the reshaped scalar path (the double test now a helper beside the SIMD loop, the per-entity splats), which every cell takes. The 8-id sitting's FAIL (load) was VISIBLE_ENTITIES +6.1 % at cv 8/7 %, the flock's spread in view, which the gather cannot reach.

**Not shipped, not pursued.** The scenes that gain read about 2 % (Predator −1.8 %, orientedBoxScene −2.3 % with the earlier form), under the 3 % a keep needs, and Boids stays 1.4–1.8 % worse in 3–4 pairs of 4. The form stays as the test module (`spatialGatherExact`). E-147 has nothing pending.

records.title: Boids physics screened: the pose epoch never reached physics (fixed, −7.2 %); W28's ceiling ~4 %
records.text:
The plan's physics item: screen `publishPose` (W15) and `applyForcesAndTorque` (W28) again on Boids, where their shares are larger than Predator's.

**The screen.** A CPU trace of boidsScene (40 000 bodies, detailed stats off, 5 s after 6 s): the physics thread is busy 414 ms/s; `publishPose` 268.8 ms in 5 s (13 %, 0.9 ms a step, 22 ns a body), `applyForcesAndTorque` 178.4 ms (8.6 %, 0.6 ms, 15 ns a body, the `body_apply_force_center` call 38 % of it).

**A bug in publishPose's way.** 42 % of `publishPose` was one line: the per-body generation load, which a fast path skips while the generation epoch has not moved since the last full publish (no body respawned). Boids never respawns, yet the fast path never ran. A probe (the skip count and the path written to two printed stat slots, not committed) showed `poseGenEpoch` null in the physics worker: the workers' buffer list (`sceneWorkerBootstrap.js`) carried `bodyGeneration` but not `bodyGenEpoch`, so physics never bound the epoch, and a spawn on a logic worker could not move it either (its box2dBodySync bound none). W15's screen blamed Predator's respawns for the fast path never latching; it never latched anywhere.

**The fix** (a412603f): the list carries `bodyGenEpoch`; `tests/node/bodyGenEpochWired.test.js` checks that the workers' buffers hold it and that a worker's spawn moves it. Every write to a body generation goes through `advanceBodyGeneration`, which moves the epoch too.

**Measured**, 4 pairs from worktrees against 95e90ce2, owner physics, detailed stats off:
- Boids: physics 7.182 → 6.669 ms (**−7.2 %**, worse 0/4, cv 2/1 %), **KEPT**; spatial +0.2 %.
- Predator gate: the first 4 pairs read physics +15.3 % (worse 3/4, cv 6/13 %) with the renderer +10.6 % and logic +4.0 %, which the change cannot reach; 4 more pairs (`--append`): over 8, physics 6.097 → 5.372 ms (−12.1 %, worse 3/8, cv 10/14 %), logic +1.1 %, spatial −1.4 %, renderer −1.7 %, pre-render −1.7 %: **NEUTRAL**, passed. Predator respawns often, so its epoch moves most frames and the fast path holds less there.

**applyForcesAndTorque on Boids:** W28's batched export would remove most of the per-body call (Node: 5.1 ns of 7.4 ns a body, R-0614); here the call is 38 % of 0.6 ms, so the ceiling is near 0.25–0.3 ms, about 4 % of Boids' physics. It needs a batch export in Box2D's repo (both builds); left as W28's lead with that number.

records.title: W28 shipped: the force and torque pass as one call into Box2D
records.text:
W28 on Boids: `applyForcesAndTorque` (8.6 % of Boids' physics thread, 15 ns a body, the per-body `body_apply_force_center` / `body_apply_torque` calls 38 % of it) as one call into Box2D.

**What shipped.** Box2D (1a750de, both builds pass `build_for_weed.bat`): `bodies_apply_accelerations(list, count, ax, ay, angularAccel, mass, inertia, isStatic, fixedRotation)`, the host's pass in C: a static body's accelerations cleared; any other pushed by body_apply_force_center with ax, ay times its mass (1 when not positive) and body_apply_torque with angularAccel times its inertia (its mass when not positive) unless its rotation is fixed; the products in float, as JS rounds them at the call. WeedJS (62eddb50): when the RigidBody columns are in Box2D's memory (the engine block), the dense body list is malloc'ed there too and the force pass calls the batch; otherwise the JS loop. A SharedArrayBuffer posted to the physics worker is another object than Module's own even when it is the same memory, so the host checks with a probe byte of its own in the heap (two markers written through the heap, read back through the column's buffer); and the build exports HEAPF32, not HEAPU8. The first sitting ran the JS fallback for those two reasons (a stat probe showed it), so it measured only the rebuilt module: Boids physics +1.7 % (worse 4/4).

**Exact.** `tests/node/bodyAccelerationsBatch.wasm.test.js`: after a step, every velocity is bit for bit the per-body calls' over static, massless, inertia-free, fixed-rotation and idle bodies; absent inertia and fixed-rotation columns read as none. `physicsFrameSteps.test.js` follows the call's new name. Node suite 2 089.

**Measured.**
- Kernel (`bodyForceCallMicrobench`, Node, the Predator fixture's 16 551 bodies; batch case c770f980): 14.1 ns a body per call, 11.8 ns in the batch (−16 %); the loop without any call 2.3 ns, so Box2D's own per-body work is most of what is left.
- Boids, 4 pairs from worktrees against b309b642, owner physics: 6.889 → 6.656 ms (−1.9 %, worse 2/4, cv 3/2 %); FAIL (load) from VISIBLE_ENTITIES (the flocks in view).
- Predator gate, 8 pairs (4 + 4 appended): physics 5.755 → 5.871 ms (+3.1 %, worse 5/8, cv 9/8 %), −0.4 % against the other workers, which all drifted up (renderer +5.0 %, pre-render +4.0 %, spatial +2.4 %, logic +1.3 %): NEUTRAL.

**Kept (kernel, product-neutral).**

records.title: E-05 sat again: pack and sort in pre-render still move Predator's bottleneck
records.text:
E-05 sat again, for EXECUTION_PLAN's "Predator's sprite statics" item: Pixi packs Predator's sprites every frame, statics included, because Predator sorts and packs in Pixi (`sortSprites: 'pixi'`, `packGpuSprites: 'pixi'`), so E-82b's split cannot skip unchanged statics. Pre-render is much faster than on 2026-10-18 (WASM: Predator pre-render −42 % steady, R-0640), so the pre-render side might take the work now.

records.title: E-159 kept: a sorted frame keeps its statics while the painter's order holds
records.text:
From the 2026-10-29 profile of the unranked pre-render and Pixi items (six scenes, `profileSceneSweep --pass cpu`): in painterSortStressScene (300 000 sprites standing, Y-sorted in pre-render, skipCull) the pre-render worker is saturated (989 ms/s), `pack_sprites_split_scatter` 49.1 % of it, and Pixi's 285 ms/s are 41 % an unnamed module (W30's `memory.copy`) and 47 % Pixi's own code.

**Why.** E-82b splits each sprite into a pose stream (16 B) and a static stream (44 B) and writes the statics only when the GPU queue buffer lacks the queue's generation; Pixi uploads them only when that generation moves. A painter-sorted frame gave generation 0: the order may move with the poses alone, and a slot's statics follow its row. So every sorted frame wrote 300 000 statics, scattered by the order, and Pixi copied and uploaded them, although nothing stood to move.

**The change** (c2e3e46a):
- The painter state carries `orderGen`, moved by a full sort or by a reinsert that moved a key; a reinsert that moved none (the same set, no key changed) leaves the order as it was, which `reinsert` in `painterRadix.c` confirms (it returns 0 before touching the order).
- `_sortedStaticGen` gives a sorted frame a statics generation of its own (bit 31 set, apart from the queue's), the same number while the queue's staticGen, the painter's orderGen, the row count and the depth scale hold, a new one when any moves; 0 when the order is not the painter's or the queue's generation is unknown. Both GPU queue buffers then hold the same number, so each writes its statics once and Pixi uploads them once.
- `tests/node/gpuPackSplitWired.test.js`: sorted frames whose keys stand rewrite the statics on the unsorted pattern and with the 15-float rows' words; frames whose keys move rewrite every time under a new generation.

**Measured**, 4 pairs from worktrees against bfd7ccf1, owner pre-render, detailed stats off:
- painterSortStressScene: pre-render 23.377 → 16.380 ms (**−29.9 %**, worse 0/4, cv 4/7 %), renderer 5.140 → 1.794 ms (**−65.1 %**, worse 0/4): **KEPT (product)**.
- painterMoveStressScene (10 % of the sprites cross a neighbour every swing: keys move every frame): pre-render −0.9 %, renderer −1.7 %, logic +0.8 %: NEUTRAL, as expected.

Predator sorts in Pixi (`sortSprites: 'pixi'`), whose path this does not change.

records.title: DX-GPCLOCK built: the sim clock keeps wall time times the scale
records.text:
The owner's call on EXECUTION_PLAN's "Left open" item "The sim clock" (2026-10-29): change it now.

**What changed** (cb72506a). `Time.simNowMs` was advanced once per main-thread frame (the wall delta clamped to 100 ms, times the scale), so a main thread that stalled froze every GPU particle while the workers, CPU particles among them, kept moving. The clock now holds a base, the wall time of that base (ms since the epoch: `performance.timeOrigin + performance.now()`, the same in every thread) and whether it runs; a reader adds the wall time since the base times `Time.scale`. The frame loop starts it, `pause()` stops it, a scale change rebases it under the sequence (now a writer lock, since any thread may set the scale), and `stepFrame` still advances a stopped clock by its injected step. `clockData` grows from 16 to 32 bytes. No worker owns it: any thread computes it.

**Tests** (`tests/node/timeScale.test.js`): a started clock runs at the scale; a hitstop or a stop freezes it with no jump; a start goes on from where it stopped; a worker thread sees it move 40 ms in 40 ms of wall time while this thread stalls. Node suite 2 092, demos 100.

**Not measured yet:** a reader now calls `performance.now()` (once a frame in pre-render and Pixi, once per `emitGpu` call). The GPU particle gate after DX-GPCLEAR, DX-GPWIND and DX-GPFOLLOW covers it.

records.title: E-160 kept (kernel): the stamp packs its grid's x and y and carries distances (Chrome -13.9 %, in the scene -11.8 %)
records.text:
**E-160: the shadow stamp on Predator's own inputs.** 2026-10-29, Wave 9.

**The tool (45505141).** `captureStampInputs.mjs` wraps pre-render's `_stampRange` through the worker's global and
records, call after call, the sun caster rows, the light table, the limits, the stamp written and the call's time.
`shadowStampReplay.mjs` replays a capture, each frame's rows in a region of their own, and folds every frame's
output into a checksum the capture's own output must match. Predator, 48 calls: 13 288–13 339 casters, 48 lights,
4 657–5 735 rows a call, 1.285 ms a call in the scene. The old fixture (one frame, 48 lights picked by hand) said
about a quarter of that.

**Where the time went** (phases cut one at a time, Node, 0.50 ms a frame): building the grid 38 % (three passes over
88-byte rows), the selection and the per-caster nearest lights 29 % (each kept caster's row read again), the append
20 %, the walk 13 %.

**The change (856cecca).** The grid build reads each row once and packs x and y in the grid's own order; a light's
walk reads them there; the walk keeps each candidate's double distance for the nearest lights; a caster row is
copied in v128s (an 88-byte memcpy is `memory.copy`, a runtime call in V8, and made the first try slower). Four
regions of the render-queue memory, table slots 28–31. The stamp is the same bit for bit: every replayed frame's
checksum is the scene's, and the node suite's parity tests pass.

| measure | before | after | |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| replay, Node (5 alternating processes) | 41.5 ops/s | 47.6 | +14.7 % |
| replay, Chrome (9 rounds) | 0.541 ms a frame | 0.466 | −13.9 % |
| the stamp in the scene, Predator (3 alternating runs a side, 480 calls each) | 1.139 ms a call | 1.005 | −11.8 %, 3/3 |
| Predator pre-render STEP_MS (4 pairs, worktrees) | 3.960 ms | 3.951 | +0.9 % paired, cv 2/1 % |

**Reading.** The kernel is faster in the scene's own call; the 0.13 ms it saves is about 3 % of pre-render, and the
sitting's pre-render read +0.9 % (pairs −0.5, +6.8, −0.4, +2.8 %). Pre-render has no wait inside its step, so the
saving is real time, under what four pairs resolve. The sitting flagged logic +4.8 % (4/4, cv 4 %), a worker the
stamp does not reach; physics read −7.6 % and the renderer −1.7 % the other way.

**Against the session's A/A** (W9-AA, Predator, 856cecca on both sides, 4 pairs): identical code read logic −1.8 %
(cv 5/4 %), spatial −1.6 %, physics −7.5 % (cv 13/6 %), renderer −3.6 %, pre-render −2.7 % (0/4 worse). Four
Predator pairs resolve about 3–4 % on these workers, 7.5 % on physics, so the sitting's pre-render +0.9 % and logic
+4.8 % (a worker the stamp does not reach) are inside its noise. **Kept (kernel), product-neutral in Predator's
STEP_MS**: the stamp itself is −11.8 % in the scene.

records.title: E-161 kept (hygiene): emitGpu calls of one frame share a group (300 movers: 18 048 -> 60 groups/s, overflows to 0)
records.text:
**E-161: emitGpu calls of one frame share a group.** 2026-10-29. Tools a87b16ee (`?trail=N` on gpuParticlesStressScene,
`gpuParticleRingProbe.mjs`), change d2827622.

A call within 8 ms of the one that opened its ring's last group joins it (records back to back, bounds widened,
earliest birth, latest end, written before the count grows and the records are published), on any layer that does
not sort with the entities and on a sorted one only for the same row; never across an epoch, other flags, past the
ring, into a group ending within 100 ms, or in a sorted look layer. A sorted group draws only what its ring uploaded.
`gpuParticleGroupJoin.test.js` checks the records are each call's own, the union of bounds, the cases that do not
join and the order of the stores; three older tests that emitted at one instant now say what they meant.

**The probe** (`?trail=300&columns=0`, 300 movers that emitGpu every tick, 5 s window), main thread's view of the
ring headers:

| layer | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| plain | 18 048 groups/s, 18 048 overflows/s | 60 groups/s, 0 overflows/s |
| sorted (each mover its own row) | 18 002 groups/s, 18 002 overflows/s | 17 940 groups/s, 17 999 overflows/s |

Records are 18 000 a second either way. Before, every call lapped a live group, so a call per entity per tick wiped
particles early; after, one group a frame. The sorted case is the documented limit (a row is a key): there, fewer,
larger calls.

**Timings.** The GPU particle gate's stress scene at its defaults is under the 3 ms floor on every worker (renderer
0.67 ms); GPU Galaxy's regression on the branch bisects to cb72506a (DX-GPCLOCK), not to this change. Kept (hygiene:
a limit fixed, nothing it reaches measured worse).

records.title: N-85, N-86, N-87 found by Wave 9's desk review and fixed (the clock's fallback, publishPose's fast path, the clock in a hidden tab)
records.text:
**N-85, N-86, N-87: Wave 9's desk review of the branch's riskiest commits, and their fixes.** 2026-10-29. A Sonnet
agent read 64899791 (E-136), cb72506a (the sim clock), 62eddb50 (W28), a412603f (the pose epoch) and c2e3e46a (E-159)

reasoning is in the agent's report: every pose change flags, the generation is loaded before any pose, ownership

- **N-86** (low): `publishPose`'s fast path read the epoch once before a loop of about a millisecond; a slot

- **N-87** (question): the clock followed wall time through a hidden tab while the workers' rAF loops stood still.
  Decided and fixed (5b01605a): `Scene.setPresenting(false)` stops the clock; the frame loop starts it again.
- A note on E-136: a kept row read between a writer's pose write and its generation bump lags one reader frame,

records.title: E-162 read: the reinsert is right for painterMove's 10 % movers; the lever is statics out of draw order
records.text:
**E-162 read: painterMove's rows, and the lever behind them.** 2026-10-29, a desk read after Wave 9's map.

painterMoveStressScene moves 10 % of its 300 000 sprites (1 in `MOVE_EVERY` drifts), so the reinsert (24 % of its
saturated pre-render) is the right tool: a full radix of 300 000 rows costs more than the moved 30 000 merged in. The
scatter pack (41 %) writes every row's pose and statics in the new draw order each frame, because the statics stream
is in draw order and any reinsert shifts it; Pixi then copies it (40 % of its time).

**The lever** is the statics out of draw order: kept in the queue's row order (or, for a scrolling camera whose rows
shift, per entity, written when an entity's statics change), with a per-frame index stream that maps draw order to
them, fetched in the vertex shader (a texture on WebGL2, as E-157 did for GPU particle records; a storage buffer on
WebGPU). painterMove would write 4 bytes of index and 16 of pose a sprite instead of 60. A scrolling scene such as
Predator gains only with the per-entity table, which needs dirty tracking of every static field. A design, not a
sitting: open until the owner says it is worth the change to the sprite batch on both backends.

records.title: E-164b kept: an entity declares only the component fields its class uses (painterMove -12.4 %, minimalTick -36.7 % against before E-164)
records.text:
**E-164b: an entity declares only the component fields its class uses.** 2026-10-29, d5213176.

**What E-164 cost.** Checked on painterMoveStressScene, whose ticks read fields of the subclass (`_drift`, `_phase`)
and no component, over 300 000 entities: 7114f7e0 against 50a2c168 (E-164), 4 pairs, worktrees: REGRESSION, logic
8.788 → 10.010 ms (+13.9 %, worse 4/4, cv 1/1 %). Every entity had grown by eight fields, and a tick loop reads every
entity's bytes.

**The change.** The constructor declares one field per component of the class (at most eight), the same sequence
for every instance of a class; `bindToEntitySlot` resets only those; a class with eight or fewer components has no
per-entity slot array (the shared empty one).

**Against the code before E-164** (7114f7e0 against d5213176, 4 pairs each, worktrees):

records.title: N-88 fixed: a subclass entity read its parent's component flags
records.text:
**N-88 found and fixed: a subclass entity read its parent's component flags.** 2026-10-29, 2f12cca0.

Found while moving the flags off the entity (E-167). `bindToEntitySlot` took `Ctor._sharedHasComponents`, a static
each class sets on itself; a subclass made after an instance of its parent read the parent's through the inherited
static, so its own components read as absent. Shown with `class Enemy { components [SpriteRenderer] }` and
`class Boss extends Enemy { components [RigidBody] }`: Boss's flags were Enemy's, `boss.rigidBody` null,
`boss._hasBox2dBody()` false (spawn and despawn read it for the body). The flags are now read only when the class owns
them; `subclassComponentFlags.test.js` fails without the fix. Kept (a fix).

records.title: Wave 9's deopt and heap passes: no deopts in eight scenes; Predator's tree tick and littleCity's rng and flowfield sample are the garbage

records.text:
**E-168 kept (hygiene): rng() steps a seeded generator's state itself.** 2026-10-29, 1971f620.

A seededRandom generator exposes its Int32Array state (`fn._state`); `rng()` reads `globalThis.rng` as before and,
when it is such a generator, steps the state in place: the same numbers, one stream with the generator's own calls
and `fill`. Any other `globalThis.rng` (a test's `() => 0.5`) is still called. In Node, 20 million calls: 34–36 ms and
6–7 scavenges, as before. (Two earlier variants behind a `globalThis.rng` accessor were 2–4× slower in Node and were
not committed.)

**littleCity, heap pass** (logic worker, KB/s): 10 573 → **6 601** (−38 %). The sites moved: CityPerson.tick 6 530 →
1 094, the generator `fn` 1 311 → gone, `rng` 1 431 → 4 201: one box left a call, the double `rng` returns to a tick
too large to inline it.

**The sitting** (littleCityScene, 0487c881 against 1971f620, 4 pairs, worktrees): logic 3.882 → 3.745 ms (−3.9 %,
worse 1/4, cv 6/3 %); spatial +0.9 %, physics +0.5 %. The runner refused it on VISIBLE_ENTITIES −12 % and

records.title: Predator's physics with Box2D's function names: the narrow phase, the solver, finalize and the tree
records.text:
**Predator's physics with Box2D's function names.** 2026-10-29, a profiling build (the shipped flags plus
`--profiling-funcs` through `CMAKE_EXE_LINKER_FLAGS`, a build directory of its own, never copied into WeedJS; the
Box2D repo's `weedjs/` artifacts it overwrote were put back from WeedJS's copies), in a worktree of 0487c881, headed,
source, detailed stats off, an 8 s window after 8 s.

Four physics threads, self time as % of their busy time: `_do_futex_wait` 65.2 % (the solver threads waiting, which the
sampler counts as busy: E-144's step 0), `b2CollideTask` 7.2 % (the narrow phase), `b2ExecuteBlock` 7.0 % (the solver's
stages), `b2FinalizeBodiesTask` 3.6 %, `_emscripten_get_now` 2.2 %, `b2ComputeFatShapeAABB` 2.2 % and `b2PlaceLeaf` 2.1 %
(the broad-phase tree for moving bodies), `step_world` 1.6 % (WeedJS's wrapper), `b2SchedulerWorkerMain` 1.4 %,
`b2SplitIsland` 1.0 %, `b2CollideCrossPairs` 0.9 %, `b2Body_ApplyForceToCenter` 0.7 %. The physics thread itself was
411 ms/s busy, the three solver threads 1000 ms/s (waiting).

What is left in physics is Box2D's own work (contacts, solver, finalize, tree). The levers are its settings (sub-steps,
the AABB margin, sleeping), a game's choice; nothing in WeedJS's wrapper stands out.

N-89 fixed: page entities could not make a component, and a hot swap reset the shared config and LogicWorker
records.text:
**N-89: two regressions of Wave 9's entity layout, fixed.** 2026-10-29, found while looking for more to drop from
the entity after E-167 (the component's `owner` stays: fsm.js reads it).

- **The page's entities could not make a component.** `Scene._createPageInstances` freezes them, and since E-164 a
  component made on its first read is kept in a field of the entity (`_c0` …). On the page, the first read threw
  "Cannot assign to read only property '_c0'": `enemy.transform`, `enemy.health.hp`, `setTint`, anything that reaches
  a component there. A page instance now keeps its components in the slot array, as every instance did before E-164;
  the logic workers' entities keep the fields (their shape is unchanged).
- **A hot swap reset the config and LogicWorker every entity shares.** E-167 put both on GameObject's prototype,
  written by the constructor. The instance hotSwap builds to list a class's fields passed `{}` and null, so after a
  swap on a logic worker every entity's `this.config` was `{}` and `this.logicWorker` null. The constructor no longer
  writes them from an instance made without them (the prototype starts with an empty config and null), and hotSwap
  passes none.

Tests: `spawnDespawnApi.test.js` (a frozen page instance reads its Transform, gets the same object twice and writes
the slot through it) and `hotSwap.test.js` (a swap leaves an entity's config and LogicWorker); both fail without the
fix. No timing: the changed lines are the first read of a component and the constructor.

records.title: DX-GPCLOCK's frames are not lost on the GPU: the same GPU time a frame, the GPU idle more, the page's frame clock slower
records.text:
**DX-GPCLOCK's frames are not lost on the GPU.** 2026-10-29, one 30 s run per side of GPU Galaxy 8M
(`particles=8388608&arms=8`, headed, source, detailed stats off; A = the branch with the clock reverted, 8471c257;
B = the branch, 1bf13c42), with the NVIDIA GPU's clock, power and use (`nvidia-smi`) and Windows' GPU engine counters
sampled about every 1.6 s (23 steady samples a side):

| | main frames | drawn | NVIDIA use | clock | power | dGPU 3D engine | iGPU 3D |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| A, clock reverted | 1 690 (56.3/s) | 895 (29.8/s) | 79.6 % | 1 669 MHz | 43.9 W | 70.4 % | 10.1 % |
| B, the branch | 1 592 (53.1/s) | 835 (27.8/s) | 74.9 % | 1 679 MHz | 41.1 W | 66.6 % | 9.6 % |

- The GTX 1650 renders (Chrome's GPU process on it at about 70 %); the integrated Radeon drives the display.
- **Same GPU time per frame** (2.67 against 2.69 % of the GPU a drawn frame), at the same clock: the branch does not
  give the GPU more work. It leaves it idle more: the page's frame clock is slower (main −5.8 %), and every worker's
  frames follow it (the gate's runs: logic and particle at main's count, the renderer and pre-render at every other
  main frame).
- So the cost is in the frame scheduling of a GPU-heavy page, and it follows how the clock moves, not how much the
  arms emit: R-0707's `?batchMs=33` took the cadence back without the frames.

records.title: DX-GPCLOCK kept with a hold: the clock moves once a main frame, its readers carry it on past 100 ms (GPU Galaxy 8M presented +6.0 %)
records.text:
**DX-GPCLOCK kept with a hold: the clock moves once a main frame, and its readers carry it on past 100 ms.**
2026-10-29, `4072de40`.

**The change.** Scene's frame loop steps the clock at each main frame (`Time._stepSimFrame`, at the frame's wall
time), by the frame's time times the scale, as before cb72506a. A main thread that gives no frame for
`SIM_CLOCK_HOLD_MS` (100 ms) does not hold it back: past that the readers carry it on at the scale, and the next frame
goes on from where they were (a stall's frame steps at least a hold, as the old 100 ms clamp gave a long frame). So
DX-GPCLOCK's point stays (a stalled page does not freeze GPU particles), and the page's frames come back.

**The sitting** W9-clock-hybrid (A = the branch at 1bf13c42, B = the change as a throwaway commit aedc04f9; 4 pairs,
worktrees, headed, source, detailed stats off, GPU Galaxy `particles=8388608&arms=8`, owner the renderer): KEPT
(product). Presented 51.8 → 54.7 fps (+6.0 %, fewer 1/4, cv 6/2 %); renderer 4.203 → 4.060 ms (−4.7 %, worse 1/4,
cv 7/2 %); logic 1.410 → 1.213 ms (under the floor: the arms' old cadence). That is the whole loss of R-0724 (−4.9 %)
and of W9-clock-share (−3.7 %), within the pairs' spread.

**Why it costs** is Chrome's frame scheduling of a GPU-heavy page, not the GPU's work (the diagnostic record): a clock
that moves with the main frame keeps the page at a higher frame rate; R-0707's `?batchMs` showed it is not the arms'
emit cadence.

Tests: `timeScale.test.js` (the clock holds between frames, steps by the frame at the scale, a hitstop and a stop
freeze it, past the hold the readers carry it on and the next frame goes on from there, N-85's fallback, another
thread sees it move while this one stalls). `npm run test:node` 2 102/2 102, `test:demos` 100/100.

records.title: E-170 kept: each component field's accessors compiled on their own (26.6 -> 8.8 ns a field access in Chrome)
records.text:
**E-170 kept: each component field's accessors compiled on their own.** 2026-10-29, 60bbe557 (kernel 20b0d11f).

**The finding** (Wave 9's second map): `get` in component.js, `return ComponentClass[name][this.index]`, is 5.2 % of
adobeAnimateScene's logic (the characters' tick) and 11.5 ms of waterAndBoxes' window. `_createInstanceProperties`
made every scalar field's getter and setter as closures of the same function literal, and V8 gives closures of one
literal one feedback vector: the keyed load `ComponentClass[name]` saw every field name of every component
(megamorphic) and the element load every column type. E-139 found the same on the entity's component getters.

**The change:** `fieldAccessors(ComponentClass, name)` compiles each field's pair with `new Function`, reading its column
by a constant name (`C["hp"][this.index]`, a named load), so each has its own feedback; if compiling throws (a CSP
without 'unsafe-eval') it falls back to the shared closures for good. `componentFieldAccessors.test.js`: each field its
own column, the current column after `initializeArrays` replaces it, a strided field has none, and the fallback with
`Function` blocked.

**The kernel** (`componentFieldMicrobench`, five entity classes' ticks reading and writing 11 fields of four game
components with Float32, Float64, Int16, Int32, Uint8, Uint16 and Uint32 columns; 2 048 entities, 200 ticks of all,
median of 7, warmed by short calls; checksum 339 388.77 on both):
- Chrome 156 (`chromeKernel.mjs`): shipped 104.6 ms (26.6 ns a field access), per field 34.5 ms (8.8 ns): −67 %.
- Node: shipped 175.9 ms (44.7 ns) before the change, 39.3 ms (10.0 ns) after it, against 35.1 ms for the variant.

**The scene:** no scene loads a worker past the floor with these reads at its defaults (Adobe's logic is 91 ms/s);
Predator gates it with E-169 (the batch's record).

records.title: N-90 fixed: hot swap of an entity class reloaded the page (E-164b), and past that broke its components
records.text:
**N-90 fixed: hot swap of an entity class reloaded the page (E-164b), and past that broke its components (E-164).**
2026-10-29, found by Wave 9's review of the day's commits (an agent's read, confirmed by running a swap of a
registered class), fixed in fc6412eb.

`instanceFields` compared the own keys of a probe of the running class with one of its new version. Since E-164b an
entity declares one `_cK` field per component of its class, counted from its registration, and the new version is
never registered: its probe declared none, so any edit to a file with an entity class answered "its instance fields
changed" and reloaded. At 844d0f20 (before E-164b) the same swap went through, and then `patchClass` copied the
probe's `_componentSlotCount` and `_componentSlotSpecs` (0 and `[]`) onto the running class: the first read of a
component not yet made threw in `_makeComponent`.

The fix compares the probes' fields without `ENGINE_INSTANCE_KEYS` (the save system's list), adds the two slot
statics to `ENGINE_STATICS`, and keeps the running prototype's `_hasComponents` (E-167). `hotSwap.test.js` now
registers a class as the engine does (the older tests fake registration), swaps it and reads a component after the
swap; it fails without the fix. No timing: the swap path only.

records.title: N-91 fixed: an emitGpu call could join a group the renderer had retired (E-161)
records.text:
**N-91 fixed: an emitGpu call could join a group the renderer had retired (E-161).** 2026-10-29, found by the same
review (reproduced there with the real emitGpu and a real GpuParticleLayerBatch in Node), fixed in 6e35e00b.

`_emit` decides the join after writing the call's records, but tested the join window and the group's remaining life
(`END_F > nowRel + 100 ms`) on the clock read at the call's start. A call whose records took long (a large burst, a
GC, a descheduled thread; at `Time.scale` 4 the margin is 25 ms of wall time) could join a group that a renderer frame
retired meanwhile; the renderer's `oldestLive` only moves forward, so no later frame drew those records. A call that
passes every other condition now reads the clock again and joins only inside the window and with the group alive past
the margin on that reading (one more clock read for joining calls only). `gpuParticleGroupJoin.test.js` makes the
second read 50 ms later and fails without the fix.

records.title: E-171 dropped: the FSM's ms per tick as a small integer (+8.3 % at 3 000 owners, a tie at 20 000)
records.text:
**E-171 dropped: the FSM's per-instance ms per tick as a small integer.** 2026-10-29, a kernel screen.

Wave 9's second map: in Predator's FSM `tick`, `let msPerTick = this._msPerTick` is 32 % of its self time. E-146
cached the owner's ms per tick on each FSM instance as a double, which pointer compression keeps boxed (a dependent
load). The variant kept the owner's `tickInterval` as a small integer and multiplied (`dt * (16.67 * ti)`, the same

records.title: N-92 fixed: hot swap kept the engine's accessors by name; now by a mark, and a class's own members are its code
records.text:
**N-92 fixed: N-90's hot swap deleted a component's field accessors, and kept old code for a member named like a
component.** 2026-10-29, found by Wave 9's second review of the day's commits (an agent's read of E-169, E-170, E-172,
E-173, N-90 and N-91, which found nothing in the others), fixed in 1b4d235f.

- `patchClass` deletes from the running prototype what the new version lacks. A component defined in the swapped
  module has field accessors made by `initializeArrays` (E-170's, or the shared ones) and `_propertiesCreated`; its
  new version, never initialized, has neither, so after the swap `new Health(3).hp` and `boid.health.hp` read
  `undefined` until the class was initialized again (a scene reload). A module of components alone did this before
  N-90 too; N-90 made modules with entity classes swap instead of reload, which reached it.
- N-90's copy skipped every key named like one of the class's components. Registration leaves a member the class
  defines under such a name in place of the component getter, so that member kept its old code through a swap, and
  one the new version removed stayed.

The fix: `engineAccessors.js` marks the accessors the engine defines on game classes' prototypes (`FIELD_GETTERS` and
the slot-array getters in gameObject.js, the field accessor pairs in component.js, compiled or shared). The swap
keeps exactly those and the engine's prototype flags (`_componentAccessorsCreated`, `_hasComponents`,
`_propertiesCreated`), and copies and deletes everything else as the class's code. `hotSwap.test.js`: a module whose
component was initialized keeps its field accessors through a swap (reads and writes the column), and a member named
like a component gets the new code; both fail without the fix. The older test's fake getter is marked as the engine's
are. No timing: the marks are made once per accessor; `componentFieldMicrobench` reads 10.6 ns a field access after.

records.title: E-174 kept (kernel): a clock read takes its frame's wall time (emitGpu 1 285 -> 625 ns a call in Chrome, trail logic -25.8 %)
records.text:
**E-174 kept (kernel): a clock read takes its realm's frame's wall time; timeOrigin read once.** 2026-10-29,
c29140c3 (kernel 77abb019).

**The finding:** a Node CPU profile of `emitGpuCallMicrobench` (E-172's kernel) put 9 % of an emitGpu call in
`Time.readSimNowInto`, with the clock stopped. In a game the clock runs, and since DX-GPCLOCK every read of a running
clock took the wall time, `performance.timeOrigin + performance.now()`. A Chrome probe (`chromeKernel`, Chrome 156):
`performance.now()` about 173 ns a call, `timeOrigin + now()` 321 ns, a typed-array read 1.5 ns. emitGpu reads the
clock once a call, and N-91 added a second read for calls that can join a group.

**The kernel** (reworked in 77abb019: browser-safe, rounds as frames, `running` starts the sim clock and notes a frame
wall each round where the tree can): Chrome, running clock, before 1 311 / 1 285 / 1 285 ns a call, after 621 / 656 /
625 (−51 %, alternated); stepped clock 672 → 604 (one run each). Node: running 756 ns before, 572–638 after.

**The change:** each realm's frame loop notes its frame's wall time (AbstractWorker._runFrame; Scene's loop through
`_stepSimFrame`), and reads take it; a realm with no frame loop (a test, a bare thread) asks the clock as before.
The hold it serves is 100 ms, far coarser than a frame: past it, a reader carries the clock on at its own frames.
`timeOrigin`, a constant, is read once per realm. N-91's second read stays: it still sees the main thread's steps
during a long call. timeScale.test.js notes the reader's frames where one thread stands for two, and checks that a
read in the same frame takes that frame's time.

**The scene** (gpuParticlesStressScene `?trail=1024`, 4 pairs, worktrees, headed, source, owner logic, A = 77abb019):
logic 1.618 → 1.201 ms (−25.8 %, under the 3 ms floor: the knob stops at 1 024 callers), renderer 3.695 → 3.596 ms
(−3.0 %, worse 0/4), presented 60.0 both. With E-172 the scene's logic went 1.845 → 1.201 ms today.

records.title: E-162 step 1: the indexed pack kernel (Chrome: a moved painter frame's pack 4.965 -> 1.400 ms at 300 000 rows)
records.text:
**E-162 step 1: the indexed pack kernel, parity-tested and measured.** 2026-10-29, d32354f8 (bench 90c67844), the
owner's go on E-162's design (EXECUTION_PLAN, 4af9f4ee).

**The kernel:** `pack_sprites_indexed_scatter` (gpuPack.c, in the engine module and the gpuPack fixture) scatters
each drawn row's pose (16 bytes) and its row number (4) to its draw slot, and, when asked, writes its statics at its
row (the queue's order, 44 bytes) with the depth term 0, for the shader to take from the draw slot.
`packIndexedRowsWasm` (gpuPackClient.js) binds it for an index list over most of the queue (as the split scatter);
nothing calls it yet.

**Parity** (`gpuPackIndexed.test.js`, two seeds, five list shapes): through the same list, the pose at each slot and
the statics at each row are the split scatter's word for word, the depth aside, which the split pack writes as
`fround(1 − (k + 1) / depthDenom)` at slot k; the pose alone leaves the statics; a frame without a list, a short
list, screen space, pixel snap, rows outside the memory and a repeated row are refused.

**The kernel bench** (`gpuPackIndexedMicrobench`, 300 000 queue rows, all in the painter's order, ms a frame):

| | split (today) | indexed, statics kept | indexed, statics written |
|---|---|---|---|
| Chrome 156, a tenth of the rows moved | 4.965 | 1.400 (−71.8 %) | 3.675 (−26.0 %) |
| Chrome 156, an unrelated order | 13.950 | 4.570 (−67.2 %) | 10.790 (−22.7 %) |
| Node, a tenth moved | 4.586 | 1.385 | 3.603 |
| Node, unrelated | 13.246 | 4.531 | 10.488 |

The pack is 39.6 % of painterMove's saturated pre-render (R-0728); the bigger share is Pixi's (40.6 % W30's copy,
41.0 % the upload), which steps 3 and 4 reach. Next: step 2 (the queue's indexed region and pre-render choosing it
where the renderer can draw it) with step 3 (Pixi on WebGL2), together, since pre-render cannot send a frame Pixi
cannot draw.

records.title: E-162 step 3 groundwork: 12-word statics rows, and the indexed vertex shader compiling and linking in Chrome
records.text:
**E-162 step 3's groundwork: the 12-word statics row and the indexed vertex shader.** 2026-10-29, 199bb5be and
3fff9b14.

- **The statics row:** 11 words do not fill whole RGBA texels, so the indexed pack now writes each row's 11 statics and
  a zero (GPU_INDEXED_STATIC_FLOATS 12, three RGBA32UI texels); the parity test checks the pad, and the kernel's time
  is unchanged (1.43 ms against the split pack's 4.64 at 300 000 rows, Node).
- **The shader:** `spriteIndexedVertex` (src/render/spriteIndexed.js) rewrites instancedSprite.vert.glsl as E-157's
  gpuParticleTextureVertex rewrote the particle shader: the seven static attributes become globals filled from three
  texels of an integer statics texture (`uintBitsToFloat`, so the packed tint, often a NaN pattern, keeps every bit),
  the row is an instance attribute (`aInstRow`), and the depth is the draw slot's,
  `1 − (uFirstInstance + gl_InstanceID + 1) × uInvDepthDenom`, the formula the split pack's depth matches exactly in
  double (the parity test). `spriteIndexedCompileCheck.mjs` (chromeKernel, Chrome 156): the shipped and the indexed
  vertex shaders both compile and link with the sprite fragment shader; the indexed program has 4 vertex attributes
  (aQuad, aInstXY, aInstRotCS, aInstRow) against 10.

Nothing is wired: the queue's indexed region, pre-render's choice and Pixi's indexed batch (steps 2 and 3) go together
next, with a Chromium pixel check (EXECUTION_PLAN.md#E-162 holds the map).

records.text:
**E-162 steps 2 and 3: indexed frames wired on WebGL, the same pixels as split frames.** 2026-10-29, wave10
(957d7b36 layout, 97e38731 painterMove's `?indexed=1`, c1e31aa9 Pixi, 4d690829 pre-render, fd34cf36 geometries).

  program from geometries of their own (gpuPackIndexedPixi.test.js). One geometry with both layouts' attributes made
  Pixi warn for each attribute a program lacks, per geometry and program, so each layout has its own and EntityChunks
  keeps up to four bases.
- **Pixels:** painterMove in Chromium, 40 lockstep steps, split against indexed: exact, 0 of 921 600 pixels differ

records.title: Pixi's own cost by layer: the upload everywhere, and Predator's decal tiles (2.2 ms of its 6.5 ms renderer step)
records.text:

have no node of their own in Chrome's profile, so `bufferSubData` is `updateBuffer`'s self time (R-0162: no copy in it).

| renderer worker, ms/s | busy | WASM (pack, copy) | Pixi `updateBuffer` | Pixi, the rest | our JS | (program) |
