records.title: N-114 fixed: the template's dev server refuses \, : and NUL paths and links out of the folder, as the engine's does
records.text:
**N-114 fixed: the create-weed-game template's dev server refuses what the engine's refuses.** 2026-11-11.

**The bug.** `packages/create-weed-game/template/scripts/dev.mjs` served `path.join(root, decoded path)` when it started with the folder.
- On Linux and macOS, `/..%5c..%5cpackage.json` was a file name inside the folder, so the server answered 404, and the test's 403 failed there.
- A link inside the game folder pointing out of it was served.

The engine's server (`server/staticFiles.js`, `resolveInside`, N-80) refuses both.

**The fix.** `dev.mjs` takes `resolveInside`'s rule, copied because the template ships alone. It answers 403 to:
- a path holding `\`, `:` or NUL;
- a path that leaves the folder once `..` resolves;
- a path that leaves it through a link (the real path of the nearest existing part).

**The test** (`createWeedGame.test.js`):
- the dev server now gets `\`, `:` and NUL paths;
- a new case puts a link out of the game folder in it (a junction on Windows, a symlink elsewhere) and asks for a file behind it, and for one that is not there. The link alone is removed before the folder.

With the old server both checks fail on Windows too. With the fix the file passes, 9 of 9.

No timing: the template's dev server is not the engine's frame. Games get the fix with the next create-weed-game release.

records.title: N-129 fixed: bullet impacts reach logic through a ring, a logic worker that misses a particle frame keeps them; bulletStressScene NEUTRAL
records.text:
**N-129's second half fixed (`54cc6109`): bullet impacts reach the logic workers through a ring, so a logic worker that misses a particle frame keeps its impacts. Hygiene keep.** 2026-11-11, from 16:02 (the sitting's first result file) to 16:05. Chrome, headed, source, detailed stats off, AC power.

**The bug.** The particle worker's bullet tick wrote each frame's impacts over the last ones, in one shared batch, and moved a sequence number. A logic worker took the batch whose number it had not seen. So:
- one that missed a particle frame (two particle frames between its reads) lost that frame's impacts;
- one reading while the next batch was written could read a mix of the two.

**The fix.** The ring is in the transport. The bullet tick (JS or bulletTick.wasm) is unchanged.
- The tick writes the frame's impacts as one batch into a private buffer.
- The particle worker appends them to a ring in the impact buffer and publishes the count. The ring (`src/util/impactRing.js`) holds eight frames of `maxImpactsPerFrame`, a power of two, after a header.
- Each logic worker runs every impact published since its own last read (`_pollImpacts`, then `processImpacts(from, to)` over the ring).
- A logic worker further behind than the ring holds runs the newest the ring still has and warns once.

**Tests** (`impactPins.test.js`, the real logic worker):
- The pins as before.
- Two particle frames before one logic frame: all three impacts run, and nothing runs twice.
- Three times around the ring, polled each frame: every impact once, in order.
- More than the ring holds between two polls: the newest ring's worth runs, from the oldest it still has, with one warning that counts the impacts lost.

**Cost.** bulletStressScene, 4 pairs (`--vs 6949e097 --hyp-rev 54cc6109 --full-rev --owner particle`): NEUTRAL.
- Particle 3.230 → 3.196 ms (-0.6 %, worse 1/4, cv 1/1 %).
- Logic 0.497 → 0.503 ms (below the floor).

N-129 is done.

records.title: N-127 fixed: a worldRect layer's float pictures are made and go up as floats on WebGL, r32float as RED
records.text:
**N-127 fixed (`7a9b646a`): a worldRect layer's float pictures are made and go up as floats on WebGL, and r32float as RED.** 2026-11-11.

**The bug.** On WebGL a float picture (`r32float`, `rgba32float`) never reached the GPU, for three reasons:
- `uploadSharedImage` handed `texSubImage2D` the picture's bytes, a `Uint8Array`, with type `FLOAT`;
- it picked `RED` only for 1-byte texels, so `r32float` went as `RGBA`;
- `createSharedTextureSource` made the picture from a `Uint8Array` too, so Pixi's first `texImage2D` (FLOAT) was refused the same way and the texture was never allocated.

WebGPU writes bytes and was right. Conurbano avoids the bug with RGBA8 in fixed point.

**The fix.**
- A float picture's upload passes a `Float32Array` over the same memory, with its offset in floats.
- A one-channel picture goes as `RED`, `r32float` included.
- A float picture starts as a `Float32Array`.

**Evidence.** A probe on a real WebGL2 Pixi renderer in Chrome 157 (through `chromeKernel.mjs`, not committed): pictures made as the engine makes them, a rectangle of shared floats uploaded twice, then read back.
- Before: `INVALID_OPERATION: texImage2D: type FLOAT but ArrayBufferView not Float32Array`, and the same for `texSubImage2D`. The framebuffer over the picture was incomplete (an attachment of zero size), and 36 of the r32float picture's floats and 144 of the rgba32float one's read back wrong.
- After: both read back exact, with no GL error.

**Tests.** `sharedTextureUploadGl.test.js` holds the call's format, type, view and offset for every format, and the first contents' type. With the old code its two float tests fail and the byte test passes.

No timing: no scene that is timed draws a float picture on WebGL. The byte path is the same call as before.

records.title: E-208 kept: list updates through a ring per logic worker; spawnStormScene with two logic workers logic -25.7 % (0/4), logic0's garbage 33 554 → 35 KB/s
records.text:
**E-208 kept: logic workers 1..N hand logic0 their list updates through a ring each, not a message a frame. spawnStormScene with two logic workers: logic -25.7 % (worse 0/4), logic0's garbage 33 554 → 35 KB/s.** 2026-11-11, from 16:36 (the sitting's first result file) to 16:39. Chrome, headed, source, detailed stats off, AC power.

**Step 0** (the scene's `?logicWorkers=N`, `3c0b5f5d`: the driver on logic1 when there are more than one, so its spawns and despawns reach logic0 as list updates). `heapSampleWorkers.mjs` on `spawnStormScene ?logicWorkers=2` (storm 1 800 a tick):
- logic0 allocated 33 554 KB/s sampled: 25 809 in `port.onmessage` (the messages' clones) and 7 705 in `_receiveListUpdates` (an object a record);
- logic1 allocated 2 157 KB/s, its driver's queries.

**The change** (`33732b3b`).
- `src/util/listUpdateRing.js` gives each worker other than logic0 a single-writer ring in shared memory: two words a record, the entity (its high bit a despawn) and its type.
- At the end of its frame the worker writes the frame's updates there and publishes them.
- logic0 drains every ring at the start of its frame into the same queues, each class from `GameObject.classByType`.
- A frame the ring has no room for goes by message as before. logic0's passes skip an index alive again or no longer alive, so the two roads' order does not matter.
- A ring holds a record for every entity (at least 4 096, a power of two): 512 KB a worker at Predator's 42 633.

**After:** logic0 allocates 35 KB/s sampled; no message and no `_receiveListUpdates` among its sites.

**Tests** (`listUpdateRing.test.js`, the real logic worker):
- as worker 1, a frame's updates go into its ring with no message;
- logic0 queues them in order, each with its class;
- nothing is read twice, around the ring three times;
- a frame with no room goes by message, and the ring keeps the frame before it.

**spawnStormScene `?logicWorkers=2`, 4 pairs** (`--vs 3c0b5f5d --hyp-rev 33732b3b --full-rev --owner logic`): **KEPT (product).**
- Logic (the worst worker, logic1) 3.160 → 2.321 ms (-25.7 %, worse 0/4, cv 2/2 %). logic1 by pair: -29.7, -26.2, -24.7, -25.2 %. The message's serialization was the writer's cost.
- logic0 0.94–1.03 → 1.01–1.11 ms (+2 to +15 %, below the floor). It now drains the rings inside its frame; the messages it used to take arrived between frames, where its step did not count them.
- Physics 2.878 → 2.942 ms (below the floor).
- BODY_COUNT +4.9 % (cv 10/16 %, the storm's emergent bodies), within the band.

records.title: N-134 fixed: raycasted lighting keeps the sun's casted shadows (Sun Street's trees and people), pre-render makes no lamp stamps or cookies for it
records.text:
**N-134 fixed (`5f1520ff`): raycasted lighting keeps the sun's casted shadows, and pre-render makes no lamp stamps or cookies for it.** 2026-11-11.

**The bug.** `initVisibilityPolygonSystem` (pixiWorker.js), which runs after `createCastedShadowsSystem`, hid the casted shadows: the shadow display sprite, `shadowSpritesEnabled` and `Layer.castedShadows.visible`. The aim was to keep the light cookies from crushing the visibility fans' umbra to black. The sun's sprite shadows went with them, so under raycasted lighting trees and people cast nothing. Sun Street runs raycasted by default. Pre-render still made the sun rows, the lamps' stamps and the cookies every frame, for nothing.

**The fix.**
- Pixi keeps the casted shadows shown under raycasted lighting and draws the sun's casters alone into them (`_castedShadowsSunOnly`): no cookie pass, no stamp pass. The fans are the lamps' shadows.
- At night, with no sun pass, the target is cleared as before.
- Pre-render makes no stamps or cookies when its visibility polygons are on.

**Evidence.** Sun Street at noon, paused (`?hour=12&paused=1`), the post-warm-up frame:
- main with `raycast=1`: houses' and cars' volume shadows only; trees, lamps and people cast nothing;
- main with `raycast=0`: every shadow;
- the fix with `raycast=1`: the same trees', lamps' and people's shadows as `raycast=0`, on WebGL and on WebGPU (`backend=webgpu`).

**Cost.** visPolyStressScene, 4 pairs, 17:21 to 17:24 (`--vs 180524cb --hyp-rev 5f1520ff --full-rev --owner preRender`): NEUTRAL, every worker below the floor. Pre-render 2.943 → 2.903 ms (-1.4 %). That scene has no casters, so the stamps it saves are not its load. In Sun Street, pre-render is 0.3 ms.

records.title: N-138 fixed: a mesh is filled at the pose its sprite was drawn at, so Sun Street's cars' volume shadows stay under them
records.text:
**N-138 fixed (`00b383fc`): a mesh is filled at the pose its sprite was drawn at, so a moving car's volume shadow stays under it.** 2026-11-11, the owner's report the same day ("the cars' shadows shake, they do not follow the cars").

**The bug.** Sun Street's cars cast with `VolumeShadowCaster`, a mesh on its own layer. The car's sprite is drawn at the pose pre-render collected into the render queue. The mesh was filled at the live Transform (`meshFillUsesLive`: a body that is static or has none, as the cars are), which logic had moved on since pre-render read it, by however many frames the workers were apart that frame: 1 to 3.

**The fix.**
- Pre-render lists, per render-queue buffer, the pose each sprite row was collected at when its entity has an active mesh (`meshPoseList.js`, written after the collect and before the emit). Only scenes with a class that has both a sprite and a mesh get the lists.
- Pixi copies the list into per-entity columns when it takes the frame, before it hands the buffer back to pre-render, stamped with the frame.
- The mesh fill (`meshFillPoseSource`) takes that pose while its stamp is the frame drawn; otherwise the latched or live pose as before (a car whose sprite was culled).
- With `renderer.interpolation` on, Pixi draws the sprite between the last two queue frames and the mesh at the newer one: a fraction of a frame apart, not measured.

**Evidence.** Sun Street filmed on main and on the fix (`?dayMinutes=60`, 16 screenshots about 200 ms apart, 16:33). Measured from the pixels: on the two rows under the white car, where the shadow box's left edge sits against the car's left edge.
- main: from −8 to −17 px over six frames (a 9 px swing, about three frames of the car's motion);
- the fix: −14 or −15 px over seven frames.

A node test with the real workers (`meshPoseFollowsSprite.test.js`): pre-render lists the car's collected pose, Pixi takes the frame, logic moves the car on, and the fill packs the sprite's pose; a frame whose list did not hold the car packs the live Transform.

**Cost.** Sun Street with 10 000 cars (`?cars=10000&dayMinutes=60`: every car a sprite with a volume, so the list holds 10 000 poses a frame), 4 pairs, 17:53 to 17:56 (`--vs 8bbdf1fe --hyp-rev 7b10560b --full-rev --owner renderer`; `00b383fc` is that commit reworded): KEPT.
- Renderer 4.348 → 3.956 ms (−9.0 %, lower in 4 of 4 pairs, cv 10/3 %). Not explained by a probe. Probably the mesh's pose now changes only with a new queue frame, so the fill's pose skip holds on the steps Pixi draws again while logic moves the Transform (Pixi drew 34 frames a second and presented 56).
- Pre-render 1.974 → 2.083 ms (+5.5 %), below the 3 ms floor and not judged: the list of 10 000 poses each frame.
- Logic, spatial and physics within 2.2 %. No A/A this sitting. Sun Street's own 6 cars write 6 entries a frame.

records.title: N-137 fixed: A* moves a cell up the heap when its cost falls; the old rule was longer than Dijkstra on 5 of 9093 grids
records.text:
**N-137 fixed (`f9cd5675`): A* moves a cell up the heap when a shorter way reaches it, so its paths are the shortest.** 2026-11-11.

**The bug.** `computePath` (particleWorker.js) kept one f a cell. When a shorter way reached a cell already waiting in the open set, it lowered that f in place and did not sift the cell up, so the heap's order broke: the cell popped late, cells reached through it meanwhile could close on a longer way, and the path could be longer than the shortest.

**Seen.** The old rule against an exact Dijkstra on 20 000 random grids of 4 to 8 by 3 to 6 cells, 70 % walkable (9093 reachable pairs): longer on 5. One of them, 6 by 4, came out 62 instead of 54; the tests keep it.

**The fix.** The search moved to `src/core/navAstar.js`, `NavScratch` with it. The heap keeps each cell's position (`heapPos`) and sifts a cell up when its cost falls (decrease-key). Each cell is in the heap once, so no extra entries, unlike the lazy entries the row planned. The heap helpers are module functions, not three closures made per path.

**Tests.**
- `astarHeap.test.js` (it tested a copy of the old rule) runs the shipped search: the grid above at 54, and 20 000 random grids against Dijkstra.
- `navComputePath.test.js`: the particle worker's `computePath` writes a 54-long path into the slot the logic workers read. On the old code it fails.

**Cost.** Not timed: no demo or stress scene requests A* paths (E-207 is waiting for a game that does), and the particle worker's frame code is the same.

records.title: astarStressScene built: 800 agents walking a maze by A*; logic 79.5 % in _findPathSlot (E-212), the particle worker half in the search (E-207)
records.text:
**astarStressScene (`671dc08e`), the owner's ask: a scene that runs A* under load, which no scene did.** 2026-11-11.

**The scene.** 800 agents (`?agents=`) walk a 96 by 96 cell maze to random cells by `NavGrid.getNextAStarPosition`, one after another.
- The maze: rooms of 12 cells with a 2-cell door in each wall and 2 by 2 pillars, as 384 static wall boxes the nav grid reads.
- Each cell an agent enters is a new (from, to) pair, so the particle worker runs A* for it. `PATHS_COMPUTED` is the load key.
- Path slots are twice the agents; every request is served the frame it arrives (`maxProcessingMsPerFrame` 50).

**Probes, src, headless, one run each:**
- 600 agents: particle 2.63 ms (27.4 paths a frame), logic 6.0 ms.
- 800 agents: particle 3.62 ms (42.2 paths), logic 10.35 ms. 800 became the default.

**The trace (800 agents, `--trace-cpu`).**
- Logic is 79.5 % `NavGrid._findPathSlot` (689 ms/s), a scan of all 1600 slot headers for every agent every tick, and 8.4 % `_requestPath`. Filed as E-212.
- The particle worker (348 ms/s):
  - the search itself, about half: `searchAstar` 29.6 %, `heapPop` 9.4 %, `siftUp`, `isVisited`, `octile`;
  - `_findExistingPathSlot` 11.1 %, another full scan;
  - `port.onmessage` 10.1 %: one postMessage for each request;
  - `allocatePathSlot` 5.0 %.

E-207 (A* in C) has its owner scene now.

records.title: E-212 kept: path slots found by an index; astarStressScene logic 11.79 -> 1.33 ms (-88.8 %), particle -13.8 %
records.text:
**E-212 kept (`501fe3ac`, sat as 36ce347c, the same tree): path slots found through an index in NavGrid's buffer, not a scan of every slot.** 2026-11-11.

**Premise (R-0889).** `getNextAStarPosition` and `getPathAStar` call `NavGrid._findPathSlot` for every agent every tick, and it read all the path slots' headers. In astarStressScene (800 agents, 1600 slots) that was 79.5 % of logic. The particle worker scanned the slots again for each request.

**The change.**
- An open-addressing index from (from, to) to slot, after the path slots in NavGrid's buffer (twice the slots, a power of two).
- The particle worker alone writes it. It lists a slot when it gives it a pair, takes it out when the slot is evicted (backward shift, no tombstones), and `invalidate` empties it.
- Readers probe it and check the slot's header (READY, from, to): a stale or moving entry is a miss, never a wrong path.
- The particle worker's request check and `allocatePathSlot`'s existing check use it.
- The pending map takes a numeric key, built only while it holds requests. A string was made on every found call.
- `navPathIndex.test.js`: 4000 allocations with 1, 3, 8 and 24 slots against the headers after each step, each slot listed once, invalidate, and a computing slot not found.

**Sitting.** astarStressScene, 4 pairs, 18:35 to 18:38 (`--vs 16c1d66e --hyp-rev 36ce347c --full-rev --owner logic`): **KEPT (product).**
- Logic 11.792 → 1.328 ms (-88.8 %, worse 0/4, cv 4/3 %).
- Particle 3.545 → 3.073 ms (-13.8 %, worse 0/4): its scan per request is gone.
- PATHS_COMPUTED 42.9 → 41.0 (-4.4 %), within the 5 %.
- Every other worker below the floor.

**Left.** In the particle worker: the LRU scan for a new slot, `_hasEmptyPathSlot`, a postMessage per request (10 %) and the search itself (E-207). No timed gameplay scene asks for A* paths, so no Predator gate.

records.text:
**E-207 kept (`a01fc243`): A* runs in navFlowfield.wasm, `astar_path` beside the flowfield, the same paths as the JS.** 2026-11-11.

**Premise.** `computePath` was the last nav search in JavaScript. In astarStressScene the search is about half of the particle worker (R-0889). The flowfield gained 16× in C (E-122).

**The kernel.** `astar_path` is navAstar.js's search (N-137's decrease-key heap) ported cell for cell: the same heap moves and the same ties, so it writes the same paths.
- A cell's open and closed marks are one generation word (2 × search open, + 1 closed) instead of the JS's stamp and its fill of `inOpenSet` over the whole grid. On the counter's wrap the marks are cleared.
- The heap keeps each place's f beside its cell, so the sifts compare without a second load.
- Its columns follow the flowfield's in the navigation memory: g, f, came-from, generation, heap, heap keys, heap places, the path. The particle worker calls it and copies the path into the slot as before.

**Parity.** `navAstarWasm.test.js`: the worker's paths equal the JS's, via a real particle worker on a scene's navigation memory.
- astarStressScene's maze, 400 pairs.
- Rubble at densities 0.2 and 0.4 with walkability 1 to 255, 300 pairs each, unreachable targets and walls included.
- Paths cut at 16 cells.
- Across the generation counter's wrap.

**Kernel** (`astarKernel.mjs`, Chrome, the maze, 2000 walkable pairs, 9 reps, one checksum for both):
- JS 109.1 µs a path.
- The first port: 36.7 µs (2.97×).
- Variants:
  - column and row passed down instead of a division per neighbour: 36.8 and 37.4 µs, a tie, not kept;
  - the heap keys beside the cells: 34.2 and 33.8 µs (3.3×), kept.
- Flags are pinned engine-wide (`-O3 -msimd128`; engine.wasm holds every kernel). SIMD and float32 do not apply to an integer heap search.
- Node screened the same: JS 109.8, WASM 37.2 µs.

**Sittings.** astarStressScene, particle worker the owner, `--full-rev`, 4 pairs each:
- Before the scene had a fixed load (`--vs d8d51e43 --hyp-rev 4f580ddc`):
  - 800 agents, 19:04 to 19:08: particle 2.764 → 1.318 ms, but its baseline was below the 3 ms floor (E-212 had cut it);
  - 1200 agents, 19:09 to 19:13: particle 4.157 → 1.995 ms (-52.0 %, 0/4), and FAIL (load), PATHS_COMPUTED 57.5 → 62.8 (+9.3 %). The agents wait for their paths, so a faster search raised their demand. Per path that sitting read 72 → 32 µs.
- The scene's fixed load since (`73dc2c45`): planners each ask for a new random pair every tick. With `?agents=0` the load is theirs alone.
- **`?agents=0`, 19:21 to 19:25 (`--vs 013b0e72 --hyp-rev a01fc243`): KEPT (product).**
  - Particle 6.770 → 2.523 ms (-63.1 %, worse 0/4, cv 1/2 %).
  - PATHS_COMPUTED 60.0 → 60.0.
  - Every other worker below the floor.

**Then the JS left src (`bcbdac0f`).** `searchAstar` moved to `tests/reference/navAstar.mjs`, the parity reference. The particle worker no longer makes NavScratch: seven per-cell arrays that neither search used, about 25 bytes a cell. It keeps the flowfield's distance cap.

**Found on the way.**
- N-139: with more paths made in one second than slots, the seconds clock evicts the path an agent is walking.
- E-214: each new path scans every slot (8000 slots: about 0.5 ms a path).

records.title: N-139 fixed: the nav slots' LRU clock counts 16 ms ticks and evictions compare ages
records.text:
**N-139 fixed (`407ea152`): the nav slots' LRU clock counts 16 ms ticks and evictions compare ages, so a path an agent walks is not evicted by a burst of new ones.** 2026-11-11.

**The bug.** `NavGrid.lruNow()` counted whole seconds. With more paths made in one second than slots, every slot held the same stamp, and `allocatePathSlot` evicted the first one, slot 0, whatever an agent was reading. Seen in Node: four slots, an agent's path in slot 0 touched, three paths nobody reads, and a fifth path the same second evicted slot 0. `allocateFlowfieldSlot` had the same clock.

**The fix.**
- `lruNow()` counts 16 ms ticks, the same in every worker. A touch still writes its slot at most once a tick (the compare-first stays).
- Path and flowfield evictions take the largest age, `(now - stamp) >>> 0`, which the u32's wrap every 2.2 years does not upset.

**Tests.** `navSlotClock.test.js`: the clock moves within a second; a touched path outlives untouched ones made the same second; both evictions across the wrap. Three of its four fail on the old code.

**Cost.** Not timed: one subtraction a slot, in the scan E-214 replaced next.

records.title: E-214 kept: path slots allocated without a scan; astarStressScene 8000 slots particle 7.045 -> 2.450 ms (-65.3 %)
records.text:
**E-214 kept (`8d28ef5b`): path slots allocated without a scan of every slot.** 2026-11-11.

**Premise.** astarStressScene with 8000 path slots: about 0.5 ms a path in the particle worker against about 0.07 ms with 1600 slots. Each new path read every slot twice: `_hasEmptyPathSlot` (a DataView read a slot) and `allocatePathSlot`'s search for an empty slot or the least recently used one. A game with many agents needs many slots.

**The change.**
- NavGrid keeps the slots never given a path since the last invalidate as a stack (slot 0 on top, refilled by `invalidate`), with their count. `_hasEmptyPathSlot` reads the count.
- Once the free slots are gone, the eviction takes the oldest stamp, by age (N-139), of eight slots from a moving hand: an approximate LRU.
- A path an agent walks is touched every tick, so it is young wherever the hand finds it. Slots another worker cleared (a save's invalidate) hold stamp 0, the oldest there is.
- `navSlotAlloc.test.js`: free slots in order and invalidate; the oldest of the sample; a path touched every tick surviving 20 000 new ones in 4000 slots.

**Sitting.** astarStressScene `?agents=0&slots=8000` (60 new paths a frame), 4 pairs, 19:31 to 19:36 (`--vs 108d649f --hyp-rev 8d28ef5b --full-rev --owner particle`; `108d649f` adds the `?slots=` knob): **KEPT (product).**
- Particle 7.045 → 2.450 ms (-65.3 %, worse 0/4, cv 1/1 %).
- PATHS_COMPUTED 60.0 → 60.0.
- Every other worker below the floor.

records.title: E-213 kept as hygiene: nav requests through a ring; particle NEUTRAL, logic 0.881 -> 0.353 ms below the floor
records.text:
**E-213 kept as hygiene (`62eebf89`): path and flowfield requests go through a ring per logic worker, not a postMessage each.** 2026-11-11.

**Premise (R-0889).** In astarStressScene's first trace, `port.onmessage` was 10 % of the particle worker, and each request cost the logic side a clone and a message.

**The change.**
- `navRequestRing.js`: a ring per logic worker in shared memory, one writer and one reader. Two words a record: a path's from and to cells, or a flowfield's target with the high bit set.
- `NavGrid._requestPath` and `_requestFlowfield` write the ring; a full ring leaves the request to the message, so nothing is dropped. The pending map keeps its dedup.
- The particle worker drains every ring at the start of its nav step, through the handlers the messages use (now methods).
- `navRequestRing.test.js`: the ring in order and full; NavGrid on the ring and on the message when full; the worker draining into its queues.

**Sittings.** astarStressScene `?agents=0`, `--vs 2bce2571 --hyp-rev 62eebf89 --full-rev --owner particle`, 4 pairs each:
- 60 paths a frame, 19:42 to 19:46: below the floor. Particle 2.419 → 2.430 ms; logic 0.422 → 0.145 ms.
- 180 paths a frame (`&plans=180`), 19:48 to 19:52: **NEUTRAL.**
  - Particle 6.418 → 6.448 ms (+0.5 %, worse 3/4, cv 1/0 %).
  - Logic 0.881 → 0.353 ms (-60 %), below the floor and not judged: about 2.9 µs a request.
  - PATHS_COMPUTED 180.0 → 180.1.

The particle worker's 10 % in that trace was the handler's work, mostly the slot scan E-212 removed, not the message. The logic side's message cost is real, small, and below the floor. Kept as hygiene: no worker 3 % worse, and no object or clone a request.

records.title: E-209 step 0: instances cost ~40 ms and 12 MB per logic worker per 100 000 slots at boot; the page 27 ms and 14 MB
records.text:
**E-209 step 0 (`83e02a98`): a pool's instances cost about 40 ms and 12 MB per logic worker per 100 000 slots at boot, and the page's frozen copies 27 ms and 14 MB.** 2026-11-11.

`entityInstanceBootMicrobench.mjs`: the real paths (`LogicWorker.createGameObjectInstances`, `Scene._createPageInstances`) on a pool of 100 000 slots of a class with two fields and a tick, a fresh class each run (cold, as a boot is). Heap is the growth after a full GC with the instances held. Node 22, two runs of 5 (medians):
- logic worker: 40.6 and 37.5 ms; 11.7 MB, 122.5 B a slot;
- page: 26.6 and 27.7 ms; 13.7 MB, 144 B a slot.

**What it means.** Per frame nothing changes. At the largest pools (524 287 slots): about 200 ms and 61 MB per logic worker, and 140 ms and 72 MB on the page. With four logic workers that is over 300 MB for slots that may never be spawned. A typical demo (10 000 to 60 000 slots) pays 5 to 25 ms and a few MB a worker.

**The change** touches 33 index reads: 21 in logicWorker.js (ticks, collision, joint and message dispatch) and 6 in gameObject.js, plus the page's API. `start()` would run at a slot's first use instead of at boot. Worth doing for scenes past about 200 000 slots. Next: the design (an `instanceAt(index)` that makes the instance on first use, the tick loops' null test measured in a kernel), queued behind cheaper items.

records.title: Predator's CPU trace on main after the day's work: logic 20 % in neighbour reads, 8.4 % in the shared tick loop (E-215 filed)
E-215 dropped at step 0: the shared tick site is ~7.5 ns a tick; the per-type lookup with .call is 46 % slower
records.text:
**E-215 dropped at step 0 (`54682d5f`): the staggered tick loop's shared call site costs about 7.5 ns a tick, and looking each type's tick up once is 46 % slower.** 2026-11-11.

`tickLoopKernel.mjs`: `LogicWorker._tickIntervalBucket` (the shipped function, a real logic worker) on four types with ticks of their own (intervals 4, 6, 6, 30; 4000 entities each, all with a RigidBody), against a copy that takes `EntityClass.prototype.tick` once per bucket and calls it with `.call`. 600 frames, 1 480 000 ticks a run, 7 alternating rounds, the same checksum. Node 22, three runs:
- shipped: 7.1, 7.6 and 7.8 ns a tick, the ticks' bodies included;
- candidate: 10.4, 11.2 and 11.4 ns (+46.3, +47.9, +46.1 %).

The megamorphic `obj.tick` is cheap. The `.call` on a polymorphic function is not. At about 5000 ticks a Predator frame, the loop's dispatch is about 0.04 ms, so its 8.4 % self time in Predator's trace (R-0898) is something else: likely the scattered reads of large instances and of the per-entity arrays, which no lookup change touches. Not taken to Chrome: a loss this size in Node is not reversed by a newer V8.

records.title: E-194 step 0: the LiquidFun scene's keyed frames are paused 589 of 600 frames (16 000 keyless rows each); it draws split
E-209 kept: instances made on first use; boot per 100 000 slots logic 40.6 -> 4.5 ms and 11.7 -> 1.5 MB; Predator NEUTRAL
records.text:
**E-209 (`b93ab8ee`): entity instances made on a slot's first use, not one per slot at boot.** 2026-11-11.

**Premise (R-0897).** Every logic worker made `new EntityClass` for every pool slot at boot, and the page a frozen copy of each, whether or not a slot was ever spawned. Per 100 000 slots: about 40 ms and 11.7 MB per logic worker, and 27 ms and 13.7 MB on the page.

**The change.**
- A slot's instance is made on its first use: a spawn, a tick, a callback, `GameObject.get`.
- At boot the logic worker writes every slot's type and "not active" for the pool at once (what each constructor wrote).
- Its maker, `_makeInstance`, builds an instance without touching the slot's Transform (the slot may be live, spawned by another worker or the page) and then calls `start()`.
- Every instance read in logicWorker.js (21: ticks, impacts, collision, joint and message dispatch, the page's despawn) goes through the maker when the slot has none. `GameObject._at` and `_instanceOf` do the same for the global and per-class lists.
- The page has its own maker: frozen instances, with the DX-GUARDS check once per class.
- `start()`, undocumented for entities and defined by no demo, now runs at a slot's first use instead of at boot.
- `lazyInstances.test.js`, on a real logic worker:
  - no instance at boot, and the pool typed and not active;
  - a slot made live elsewhere gets its instance on its first tick, with `start()` once and its Transform left alone;
  - `GameObject.get` makes one; an index outside the pools gives none;
  - the page makes none until asked, frozen.

**Boot** (`entityInstanceBootMicrobench`, 100 000 slots, Node 22, two runs of 5):
- logic: 40.6 / 37.5 → 4.5 / 4.7 ms; 11.7 → 1.5 MB (16 B a slot: the index arrays);
- page: 26.6 / 27.7 → 1.4 / 1.3 ms; 13.7 → 1.5 MB.

**Per frame: Predator's gate**, 4 pairs, 20:30 to 20:34 (`--vs 504d9bdf --hyp-rev b93ab8ee --full-rev`): **NEUTRAL.**
- Logic -7.5 % (worse 0/4; -7.8 % against the others, lower 4/4).
- Spatial +2.7 % (3/4), pre-render +0.1 %, physics +4.5 % (2/4): workers the change does not reach.
- No page error.

The tick paths' `??` costs nothing while a slot has its instance.

Kept for boot and memory. Per 100 000 slots, each logic worker saves about 36 ms and 10 MB and the page 26 ms and 12 MB; at the largest pools, over 250 MB with four logic workers. Instances are now made as slots are used, a spawn burst paying them then.

N-140 fixed: the cull pads each sprite with its reach from its anchor (houses and trees no longer vanish at the edge)
records.text:
**N-140 fixed: the cull pads each sprite with its reach from its anchor.** Reported 2026-11-12 by the owner from The Chaos Machine (another developer's game on 0.14.0): houses and trees disappeared at the screen's bottom edge while their tops still showed.

- **Cause:** the collect padded the view with the larger half bound around the pose; a sprite anchored at its foot (the default 0.5, 1) reaches its whole height above it. A 293×262 house was dropped with 43 px of it on screen at zoom 1, 159 px at zoom 2.
- **Fix (`93aacc8d`):** the pad is the distance from the anchor to the farthest corner (`src/util/spriteCullReach.js`, the same in `preRenderCollect.c`), turns and flips included; the kernel tests a pose inside the view first and reads the anchors only for one outside it; the static scenery grid widens by the largest reach; `setAnchor` re-bins a static sprite.

records.text:
**E-217 kept: the collect keeps its copy of the sprite query's list while nothing was published.** `ef03a7a1`.

- **The knob:** `?lf=<n>` sizes LiquidFun's maximum and the queue and spans the basin with the box (147 px² a particle, from y 2400 up). At 60 000 every particle is on screen (QUEUE 60 000); physics then takes about 100 ms a step.

**liquidFunQueryStressScene `?lf=60000`, owner renderer, 4 pairs, `--vs eff1d339 --hyp-rev 13f47e9c --full-rev` (02:21 to 02:27):** NEUTRAL (below floor) by the runner.

- Pre-render 3.411 → 3.741 ms (+8.0 %, worse 4/4, cv 7/5 %).
- Physics -2.1 % (cv 65/5 %), the others under the floor.

**One CPU trace a side** (headed, 8 s warm-up, 6 s, `--trace-cpu`):
- Pixi 191 → 97 ms/s busy: `pack_sprites_split` 54.5 → `pack_sprites_keyed` 21.1 ms/s, `updateBuffer` 47.6 → 15.5.
- Pre-render 222 → 255 ms/s: `emit_rows` 75.3 → 103.1 ms/s, about 7.7 ns for each of 3.6 million LiquidFun rows a second. The rows come in particle order, so the records are read in order: one more stream of 1.9 MB a frame on top of the dozen the emit reads, and the prefetchers do not hide it.

A dense u16 per particle (120 KB) holds the compare epoch it was last checked at; the emit skips the 32-byte record when it equals the current one, which moves when Pixi asks for every statics again or physics says a LiquidFun static may have changed (a paint, a count that moved, a fading group). records.title: N-142 fixed: LiquidFun's render statics follow the particles through compactions, joins, extractions and splits
records.text:
**N-142 fixed: LiquidFun's render statics follow the particles through LiquidFun's reorders.** Engine `3cbb90eb` (branch `fix/n142`), Box2D `Box2d_3.2` `7a1d29b`.

- **Reproduced first** (a probe page, not committed: headless Chromium, WebGL, two box emits of 0xff0000 and 0x00ff00, the red with a 1.5 s lifespan, no gravity). Red and green pixels in each half of the canvas:
  - at 0.8 s: left red 3 381, right green 3 381;
  - at 4.8 s, after the red died: left nothing, right **red 3 381, green 0**. The green particles slid down into the red ones' indices and took their tint.
- **Cause:** LiquidFun compacts its buffers when particles die (and rotates them on a join, permutes on an extraction, copies on a split); its own buffers follow each particle, but the render buffer's tint, texture, scale, rotation, base alpha and layer mask are painted once by index when a particle is made.
- **Fix:**
  - Box2D: each particle's `originIndex` (its index at the last `lfParticleSystem_ResetOrigins`; a new particle its own) is carried through `CopyParticle`, `PermuteParticleRange`, `RotateBuffer` and the split's copy, with a `reordered` flag. Exports `get_particle_origin_byte_offset`, `particle_reordered`, `reset_particle_origins`. Both builds (SIMD and no-SIMD) pass `build_for_weed.bat`.
  - Engine: `followLiquidFunReorder` in the physics host, after each frame's steps and after a join, a split or an extraction, moves the eight render-statics arrays from each particle's origin (in place for a compaction, which only moves particles down; from a copy otherwise), then resets the origins.
- **Checks:** `liquidFunOrigins.wasm.test.js` (a compaction: every survivor's origin is where it came from, and green; a join: each particle is the one at its origin). The probe after the fix: at 4.8 s right **green 3 381, red 0**. Node 2490 of 2490, demos 101 of 101.
- **Left:** pre-render's previous LiquidFun positions (`_prevLfX`, the interpolation) are latched by index, so a compacted particle interpolates from another's position for one frame.

**Gates** (src, headed, AC power):
- **liquidFunQueryStressScene**, owner physics, 4 pairs, main vs the branch (02:54 to 02:59): NEUTRAL. Physics 11.241 → 10.994 ms (-1.2 %, worse 2/4, cv 2/3 %); the rest under the floor. (Its queue then held 16 000 of 19 656 particles; fixed since in 00b1448f.)
- **Predator**, 4 pairs (02:47 to 02:53): NEUTRAL by the runner, physics 5.105 → 5.786 ms (+11.4 %, worse 3/4, cv 15/9 %) on a scene without LiquidFun. The Box2D binary grew 575 bytes (the three exports), the same build as main's.
- **Predator again, 8 pairs** (`--name n142-predator --vs d0455d75`, 03:02 to 03:09): NEUTRAL. Physics 5.682 → 5.639 ms (-4.8 %, worse 3/8, cv 22/16 %; pairs +2.3, +6.4, +23.4, -5.6, -6.5, -11.6, -12.4, -4.0), logic -4.1 %, spatial -2.3 %, pre-render -2.6 %. The first sitting's +11.4 % was noise.

**Verdict: kept (hygiene).** A bug fixed, no primary worker 3 % worse.

records.title: N-143 fixed: the camera follows an entity without a body by its Transform (ported from networking_cars)
records.text:
**N-143 fixed: the camera follows an entity without a body by its Transform.** `3d370959`, merged in the fix/n143 merge; ported from networking_cars `2dc726e3` (2026-10-26), which main never got.

- **Cause:** `Camera.followEntity` held the camera while the physics publish frame was unchanged, and the drawn camera snapped to the followed entity's latched pose slot. Only bodies have one: an entity without a body read 0, 0 (the view at the world origin), and with every body asleep the publish frame never changed, so the hold never ended.
- **Fix:** both rules for bodies only: `_alignToSnapshot` returns the SAB camera for an entity without an active RigidBody, and `publishFrozen` needs a body.
- **Checks:** `cameraFollowBodyless.test.js` fails 2 of 4 on main's camera (the two bodiless cases) and passes with the fix; the camera tests 33 of 33; Node 2501 of 2503 in a worktree without node_modules (pixiDrawGarbage and pixiShaderSync import a file inside node_modules by path), demos 101 of 101.
- Hygiene, nothing to time (a test per followed entity a frame).

records.title: N-144 fixed: asset fetches and their body reads tried once more past the HTTP cache
records.text:
**N-144 fixed: an asset fetch and its body read are tried once more past the HTTP cache.** `b82561fe`, merged in the fix/n143 merge.

- **Cause:** two tabs of one browser loading the 16 MB roads tilemap at once failed one with `net::ERR_CACHE_WRITE_FAILURE`: the body read rejected though the server had answered. networking_cars retried tilemaps (`36870ce0`, `fetchRetry.js`); main loads every asset through `fetchAsset` (DX-GUARDS C6), which did not retry, and its callers read the body after it returned.
- **Fix:** `fetchAssetRead(url, what, read)` fetches and reads; on a network failure of either (a TypeError) both once more with `cache: 'no-store'`. An HTTP error and a body the caller rejects (bad JSON) are answers, not retried; the errors keep C6's wording. `fetchAssetJson` reads through it; the baked bigAtlas PNG, a tileset, a sound and a worker's image now read inside it.
- **Checks:** `fetchAsset.test.js` (the branch's four cases: a failed request, a failed body read, an HTTP error and bad JSON not retried, a second failure named), 8 of 8. A cache write failure cannot be made in Node or headless Chromium on demand: the retry is tested with a fetch that fails as it does.
- Hygiene, nothing to time (asset load only).

In headless Chromium: "Cannot read properties of null (reading 'buffer')" at `initializeCoreEntityAndComponentBuffers` (sceneSharedBuffers.js): with zero entity slots `createSpatialPublishMemory` lays out nothing and returns null. With that worked around, the physics host stopped at "init missing Transform/RigidBody/Collider buffers".

records.title: N-141 fixed: decorations culled with the pool's largest reach as a margin; Predator NEUTRAL
records.text:
**N-141 fixed: decorations are culled with the pool's largest reach as a margin.** `594ed8a2`.

- **Cause:** the particle worker's decoration screen test reads one point a decoration (its position against the view plus `cullingRatio`), so a large decoration drawn from its foot went missing at the bottom edge with its top still on screen (and at the sides for an anchor off centre). Filed fixing N-140; the guide advised cutting tall decorations into pieces.
- **Fix:** the pool keeps the largest reach any decoration has had from its position to the far corner of its sprite (frame × |scale| from the anchor, as `spriteCullReach` does for sprites, plus the draw offset), rounded up, in word 3 of its list header (`DECORATION_MAX_REACH`): `DecorationPool.noteReach` at spawn (before the list shows the decoration) and in the facade's scale, anchor, texture and offset setters; `despawnAll` resets it. The particle worker pads the decorations' screen test with it (`_decorationCameraBounds`, all four paths: both loops, the flip sample, the hold check), so the per-decoration loops (E-179) read nothing more.
- **Checks:** `decorationReach.test.js`: the reach (anchor, a flip, the offset); a 600 px decoration whose foot is 300 px below the view kept, one past its reach not; growing one raises the pad and the test runs again; despawnAll resets. The two screen cases fail without the pad. In Predator (a probe, the real bigAtlas sizes) the grass reaches 71 px. Node 2519 of 2519, demos 101 of 101.

**Predator's gate, 4 pairs** (`--name n141-predator --vs main --hyp-rev fix/n141`, 05:26 to 05:33): NEUTRAL. Spatial -2.1 %, physics -4.2 % (0/4 worse); logic -1.5 %, renderer -2.9 %, pre-render -4.0 %, particle -5.1 % (under the floor); load keys within 0.1 %.

records.title: E-197 built: input-to-screen latency stamp; Boids 67 ms (4 frames) from an input to its frame; Predator NEUTRAL
records.text:
**E-197 built: the input-to-screen latency stamp.** `da79c6fb`, a tool (no speed claim).

- **What it measures:** for each input (keys, pointer) the time to the first frame Pixi draws with it. Main stamps the input (tenths of a ms since a base every thread shares, one Int32 in the scene's stamp buffer); logic0 publishes the input its last frame acted on; physics carries the stamp it stepped with into the pose slot it writes (`poseSync` gains a stamp a slot); pre-render writes the newer of logic's and the latched pose's into the render-queue buffer it fills (its camera SAB gains a word, 20 → 24 bytes); Pixi's `LagMeter` (the last 64 inputs drawn) publishes `RENDERER_STATS.INPUT_LAG_MS`, `INPUT_LAG_P95_MS`, `INPUT_LAG_N` (stride 39 → 42). `runIntegratedWorkerBenchmark --input-every <ms>` moves the mouse over the canvas and prints the lag on the renderer line.
- **First reading:** Boids, headless, a move every 100 ms: **67.1 ms median, p95 68.1 ms, 4.03 frames at 60 Hz**, as E-24's reading said (each stage reads what the one before it published a vsync earlier).
- **Checks:** `latencyStamp.test.js` (the clock, main's stamp, the meter's samples and percentiles, the queue's stamp word, the stats slots); the camera SAB and stats stride tests follow the new sizes. Node 2523 of 2523, demos 101 of 101.

**Predator's gate, 4 pairs** (`--name e197-predator --vs main --hyp-rev tools/e197`, 06:01 to 06:07): NEUTRAL. Spatial -1.1 %, physics -4.3 %; logic, renderer, particle and pre-render under the floor, all lower. The stamp is a few atomic loads and stores a frame per worker.

**Next:** E-198, judged by this.

records.title: E-198 step 0: no link waits in Boids; input lag 3 frames (50 ms); the waits built change nothing; the meter was a frame high
records.text:
**E-198 step 0 answered: in Boids no link of the frame chain waits for the one before it; the input lag is 3 frames, and the waits built for it change nothing.** Branch `speed/e198` (`3d36cfad`), not merged.

- **First, the meter was a frame high.** logic0 published the input its frame had acted on at the next frame's start, so a stage that ran after logic in the same vsync read a stamp a frame old with this frame's data. Fixed on main (`5434da27`: published from `afterUpdate`, a hook abstractWorker calls right after `update()`): Boids, a move every 100 ms, **67.1 → 50.6 ms median (4.03 → 3.04 frames)**; the code drawn did not change. R-0924's figure was the meter's.
- **Where the 3 frames are** (a temporary probe logging each stage's input age, not committed; Boids, headless): logic reads an input **16.1 ms** after it arrives (about a frame: Chrome dispatches pointer events aligned to its frame and logic's frame has started); pre-render latches a pose stepped with it **48.7 ms** after it (two frames after logic read it); Pixi draws it at **50.4 ms**, 1.7 ms after pre-render queued it (no frame lost there).
- **The waits built** (each with a budget, the frame less its own step and room downstream, and a timeout that turns it off for 120 frames, counted in WAIT_MS): Pixi for pre-render's queue (`renderer.waitForQueue`), pre-render for physics's pose (`preRender.waitForPose`), physics for every logic worker's frame end (`physics.waitForLogic`, a frame-chain counter the logic workers add to in `afterUpdate`). In Boids **none of them waits**: each stage's upstream is out when its frame starts (no WAIT_MS on physics, pre-render or the renderer), and the lag stays **50.4 to 50.5 ms**.
- **Reading:** the premise (each link reads the previous vsync's output because the workers start together) does not hold in Boids: the stages already run one after the other within the vsync's reach, and the two frames between logic and pre-render are not waits. Node 2523 of 2523 on the branch.

**Next:** the frame clock (E-24's `frameClock`, each worker's frame start and end in wall time) laid out as a timeline for a few frames, to see each stage's phase against the vsync and where the two frames between logic and pre-render go; then decide what to change (the stages' phases, or physics's pose publish). The meter stays (E-197).

records.title: E-198 kept: the frame chain within one vsync; input lag 51 -> 24 ms in Predator and Boids, workers' own time -20 to -36 %
records.text:
**E-198 kept: logic, physics, pre-render and Pixi chained within one vsync; an input reaches the screen about 27 ms (1.6 frames) sooner.** `08a689ce` (the change), `a48db56a` (its test), merged in the speed/e198 merge.

- **The premise, now measured:** `runFramePhase` (`--scene`, `7ed115ad`) on Boids: every worker wakes within 0.2 ms of the others ("wake-together"), so each stage reads what the one before it published a vsync earlier. E-197's meter: 50.4 ms (3 frames) from an input to the frame drawn with it.
- **Why R-0925's waits never waited:** they waited only when nothing newer than the last read was out, but when the stages wake together there always is (the upstream's output of the vsync before). The waits now wait for an output of **this** vsync: physics for every logic worker's frame end (a frame-chain counter each adds to in `afterUpdate`), pre-render for a pose newer than the one out at its start, Pixi for a queue newer than the one out at its start, then drawn. Two more found on the way: pre-render marks the pose out at its start consumed before it waits (physics holds its publish until the last pose is consumed, `posePublishBlocked`: the wait always ran out), and physics answers sync queries between 0.25 ms slices while it waits (a logic worker blocked on a ray finishes its frame only once physics answers, and the idle wake cannot run under an `Atomics.wait`).
- **Budgets and fallbacks:** each wait at most the frame less its own step and room downstream (physics 6 ms, pre-render 4 ms); a timeout turns that stage's waits off for 120 frames. Waits go into `WAIT_MS`. `physics.waitForLogic`, `preRender.waitForPose`, `renderer.waitForQueue` (true) turn them off. On Windows an `Atomics.wait` timeout can overrun to the timer's ~15 ms: a stage whose wait runs out may miss one vsync, then waits no more for two seconds.
- **Checks:** `frameChainWait.test.js` (Pixi and pre-render wake on their upstream's publish, the pose marked consumed, the wait in `WAIT_MS`, a timeout turns the waits off; a second thread publishes). Node 2527 of 2527, demos 101 of 101.

**Sittings, 4 pairs each, `--vs main --hyp-rev speed/e198 --input-every 100`, src, headed, AC power (06:47 to 07:07):**
- **Predator** (NEUTRAL by the runner, no owner): input lag 51.6, 51.5, 51.7, 51.5 → 27.0, 24.7, 24.7, 24.6 ms; STEP_MS − WAIT_MS spatial 3.745 → 2.897 ms (-21.1 %), physics 4.402 → 3.242 (-26.0 %), pre-render 2.877 → 1.802 (-36.3 %), renderer -30.5 %, logic -27.4 % (worse 0/4 each; particle +7.7 % under the floor); frames presented 59.99 both.
- **Boids** (owner spatial): **KEPT (product)**: spatial 5.316 → 4.185 ms (-20.9 %, worse 0/4), physics -25.9 %; input lag 50.3 to 50.6 → 23.2 to 23.5 ms (p95 51 → 24); frames presented equal.
- **liquidFunQueryStressScene** (sync queries every tick, owner physics): NEUTRAL, physics -1.7 %; input lag 50.4 → 35.0 ms; frames presented equal.

The workers' own time fell too: they no longer all start their work together on the vsync, so they contend less for the cores (spatial, which waits for nothing, read -21 %). A short test run overlapped part of the Predator sitting.

**Verdict: kept.**

One scene's CPU trace: self and inclusive time, hot lines, callers.
Deopts and megamorphic ICs after warm-up, ranked by count × self time.
Allocation per site in KB/s, per worker, in Chrome (Node does not show Chrome's boxing).
Kernels timing OSR code; fields whose V8 type is Any.
Push entities or particles until a worker saturates: what saturates first is the next target.
Open review items (bugs and cleanups found while reading code).

A drop decided on a floor, on a drift every worker shared, on a sitting that was contaminated or served from the main folder, or in a regime that cannot show the gain: reopen it as a new entry that points at the old one (E-123 to E-128 did).
